ME. HELLYER    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting the members of this house. Yesterday in reply to a question from the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) is quoted in this morning's Globe and Mail as having said:
There have been reports indicating that some manufacturers and vendors of some products affected by the commodity tax changes announced in the budget are raising prices to the public and increasing them inexcusably by amounts in excess of the increase in the tax.
In Hansard of April 16, Mr. Speaker, the same part of the Prime Minister's reply is as follows:
There have been reports indicating that some manufacturers and the vendors of some products affected by the commodity tax changes announced in the budget are raising prices to the public, and increasing them by amounts in excess of the increase in the tax.
In the interests of clarity and accuracy, Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister should tell the house which report is correct.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FOOD FOR PEACE CONFERENCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER AS TO MEETINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in my reply to the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition on Tuesday in connection with the food for peace conference, the Canadian government has accepted an invitation to participate in the meetings with representatives of the United States and other major wheat exporting countries to consider the proposals outlined in the President's farm message to congress on January 29. The invitation was extended by the United States secretary of agriculture, Mr. Benson, to whom the President entrusted the task of pursuing the proposals which he advanced in his message. The other countries taking part will be Australia, Argentina and France. The director general of the food and agriculture organization will also be present.
The meetings will take place in two stages. Officials will meet from April 27 to April 29 to prepare material for consideration at a ministerial meeting on May 5. In his address to congress the President proposed that a new approach should be made to endeavour to make better use of the free world's agricultural abundance in the interests of reinforcing peace and the well-being of friendly peoples throughout the world; in short, to use food for the purposes of advancing peace and
2788	HOUSE OF
Proposed Food for Peace Conference peaceful objectives. The United States suggested that attention might be turned first to problems in wheat distribution and indicated that at a later date consideration might be given to other agricultural commodities. It is proposed at these meetings to review problems affecting products and trade in wheat and surplus disposal programs now in effect. Consideration will also be given to the possibilities of improving present programs in order to make more effective use of current agricultural surpluses.
I need hardly add to what I said the other day, namely that the Canadian government is wholeheartedly in support of the objectives outlined in the President's address and welcomes the opportunity to discuss problems in wheat distribution and marketing with other major exporting countries. The suggestions I have made on other occasions looking to the establishment of a food bank for the assistance of countries whose populations are short of necessary food, either because of crop failures or natural disasters or for long term reasons such as economic underdevelopment, were directed to very much the same objectives as those outlined by the President. The Washington meetings will provide an opportunity to examine these suggestions as well as other suggestions put forward, and the Canadian representatives will endeavour to play a constructive role in seeking to advance the humanitarian objectives outlined by the President.
The success of any food for peace program will depend on finding ways to increase consumption in the food deficit countries. At the same time they will seek to ensure that in any proposals that may develop, adequate provisions are made to ensure that normal commercial markets are safeguarded. The elaboration of detailed proposals is not an easy task, and I should like to endorse the remarks of Secretary Benson that soundness of approach is essential and should take precedence over speed, important as speed is.
The Canadian government will be represented at the ministerial level on May 5. The composition of the Canadian delegation to the two meetings will be announced shortly, and the house will be given full information as to the results of these meetings. I think that is about as far as I can go at this time in answer to the hon. gentleman's question. I hope I will be in a position almost immediately to announce the composition of the delegation.

I am very pleased that it is to take place, because for many years when others were laying great emphasis on the United States export program I was saying that instead of making such loud protests it would probably be more effective if we were to sit down in conference with the United States and other countries involved to work out a common program to deal with this common problem.

The Leader of the Opposition said that a recent return showed what chaotic conditions can be brought about when exports are subsidized. In the international situation today I believe that food is more important than ever. It is important not only in the sense that it must be made available to people who are hungry and in great need, but I also believe it is an important instrument in the arsenal of democracy, an instrument that may be used to feed undernourished people and in turn help underdeveloped countries improve their economies. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NUCLEAR TESTS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT CONCERNING U.S. AND U.K. PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked as to whether I could comment on recent press reports concerning the proposals made by the United States and the United Kingdom at the resumed negotiations in Geneva on nuclear tests. In reply I wish to advise that the Canadian government has been informed of the stand taken by the United Kingdom and United States representatives at the Geneva negotiations with respect to the approach they are making to the Soviet representations at that conference.
What is perhaps not clear from some of the published reports is that the western powers have not proposed abandoning the attempt to reach a comprehensive agreement and of substituting for it an agreement confined to nuclear tests in the upper atmosphere. They
Atomic Energy-Nuclear Tests have proposed that the main effort continue, but that since the major stumbling block has been the question of on-site inspection in the case of unidentified subterranean events, and since discussion last summer of the techniques of detection in outer space was not pursued to agreed technical conclusions, as an interim measure the existing area of agreement might be consolidated. The negotiations would then continue with respect to explosions underground and in outer space.
This suggestion was put forward by the two countries as an alternative procedure. If the Soviet union were not for the present prepared to change its position on the veto in respect of procedures for on-site inspection and on early discussion of practical measures for high altitude detection, at least the alternative proposed, if implemented, would provide the means for avoiding further contamination of the atmosphere with artificial radioactivity should the nuclear powers decide to resume weapons tests. It would also enable a start to be made on the establishment of a control system. It would, however, leave for the future the achievement of the important objectives of arresting competition in the development of nuclear weapons and in restricting the capability of manufacturing them.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, the other day when he was in Hamilton at the inauguration of the first reactor in Canada, the Prime Minister expressed the hope that some constructive results would be achieved in the vitally important discussions that are now taking place in Geneva on nuclear tests, and perhaps the reception to or the results of these new proposals will indicate whether these hopes are to be realized.
These new proposals do run the risk of being misinterpreted, misrepresented and indeed distorted by those who are opposed to any international action in this field. This risk is the greater because of certain statements that have been made in Washington during recent months to the effect that underground tests cannot be detected by any control agency although, I should add, there are other United States experts who have denied this. This is one of the reasons, of course, for the confusion of laymen in a field of this importance. But the confusion which does exist has given ammunition and argument to the opponents of a ban of all tests in the U.S.S.R. and in the U.S.A.
I realize, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, that the Russian position in regard to control and inspection, which are a vital part of this whole effort, has been intransigent

Inquiries of the Ministry on their insistence on the use of the veto. I suggest, however, and perhaps this is a point which will be in the minds of those who are taking part in these discussions, that perhaps the western position would be stronger in reply to this Russian position if there could be no big power representation of any kind on any control agency which might be set up, and if that could be left to the United Nations where it could be effectively done.
This new proposal, Mr. Speaker, I hope will not toe interpreted by public opinion in any country as a withdrawal from the ultimate position which the west has taken, to the effect that all nuclear tests must be banned. If this could be put forward as a stage, it might be easier for the Russians to accept because the ban would be confined to atmospheric tests. Some of the controls which would be required in other forms of tests would not be necessary here. If it could be put forward in this sense, as one stage, it might be useful and helpful in the achievement of the ultimate objective of a total ban. If, however, it is going to be misinterpreted and misrepresented as a departure on our side from that ultimate objective, then, Mr. Speaker, we shall all suffer.

The C.C.F. for years has taken the position that nuclear tests should be abandoned. Of course the best possible arrangement is to have international control and inspection. I think there is a growing body of evidence that continuing nuclear tests endanger the very existence of mankind. The position Canada should take is that we should encourage and endeavour to persuade all nations in the world to cease nuclear tests. I myself feel very strongly that the western nations should take this lead, and should say to the Soviet union, "our testing is over", that we should cease testing nuclear weapons, particularly on this continent, at least until such time as we see what action or what measure of co-operation will be forthcoming from the Soviet union after we have said that our nuclear tests are ceasing.
There is disturbing evidence that the increase of strontium 90 is endangering human welfare and could lead to very serious results for the human race in generations to come. I submit that Canada has an opportunity to take the lead by insisting on ceasing and endeavouring to persuade all nations to cease nuclear tests.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seem to be getting a fair amount of exercise today in rising and sitting down. Last evening as we were approaching ten o'clock I had begun to relate my opinion as to the attitude which exists in Canada today regarding the effect that wage increases may have upon price increases. I had said there were varying opinions, some to the effect that the workingman is completely to blame. Others are more enlightened, and say that while wage increases may have had some effect there are also other causes.
I mentioned that the hon. member for Acadia in his discussion of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, had left the impression that the rising level of wages in the agricultural implement industry was directly responsible for the increases in the prices of farm machinery. He made reference to a 6 per cent increase instituted by the farm implement companies last fall, and left the impression that this was the direct result of an increase in wages paid to employees working in the agricultural implement industry.
I would point out that in this instance I do not think the comparison is quite correct. The real reason that prices were increased was the Tories' $1 an acre program and the fact that the farm machinery manufacturers wanted to capitalize on this extra income. With respect to the movement of farm machinery prices, it is a pretty well-known fact that for at least 50 years some sort of price fixing arrangements have existed in the agricultural implement field and that there has been relatively little competition and in many years no competition in the prices for farm machinery. In fact in 1937 a committee of the house considered the question of farm implement production, and one conclusion it came to was that there had been little or no competition in the farm implement industry for quite a number of years.
We know that annually for at least the past five years and probably for some number of years before that the companies in the farm implement industry have been making regular and almost automatic increases in the prices of the machinery they sell, amounting to approximately 6 per cent each year. I have some statistical information compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics respecting average annual hourly earnings in the agricultural implement industry. I am only taking the figures from 1953 to 1958, as

being relatively recent. Over that five-year period we find that wages increased in this industry by 18.01 per cent, but we also find that the prices charged by the agricultural implement industry increased by some 30 per cent. That means twice as much increase in price percentagewise as compared with the increase in wages over that same period.
At one time it used to be quite popular to be against sin. Then there was an anti-Quebec feeling; people from Quebec were on the short end of the stick. The Jewish people have been subjected to the same sort of thing. It was popular to be against communism. Now it is popular to be against unions, or anti-union. The spread of this propaganda of an anti-union nature takes many people down a blind alley and leads them to the conclusion that anything which unions do is of no value and should be condemned. I know from personal experience, as I related to some extent during last year's debate on departmental estimates-and I intend to comment also on this at a later stage in the proceedings-that unions sometimes do things which are not too sensible and which we should not regard as too helpful to our economy. It is true that in some negotiations which have been conducted by the unions, their attitude, approach and demands are sometimes just not reasonable. But that does not give us the right to condemn everything the unions do.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to relate two or three instances where international unions have acted in a manner which is most responsible toward society, and whereby they gave full consideration to the effect of their negotiations upon other sections of society apart from those in which they were directly involved. I would like to relate an instance of an attitude which has been prevalent in the united packing house workers of America for some years. Negotiations between the U.P.W.A. and the packing house industry have an effect on farmers, and for some time the packing house workers in their negotiations with the meat packing industry have asked the industry to guarantee a certain floor price to the farmers for the commodities the meat packers buy. They have been concerned enough about the farmers to attempt to protect them as much as they can in that way, but they have been told time after time by the meat packing industry to mind their own business. They said, "The price we pay the farmer for hogs or other animals which we buy has nothing to do with you." So the U.P.W.A. has expressed this desire to protect the farmers and the commodities they sell to the meat packers of Canada, but they have been told it is none of their business and that they should pay 66968-9-1785

The steel workers union suggested that they would be prepared to co-operate with the government in any way if the government would institute such an investigation and study; and if it was discovered that wages paid to the steel workers were pushing up steel prices, the steel workers' union would take that into consideration in its negotiations for wages and it would affect the wages paid in the steel industry. They are asking for an independent survey because they do not know what the position is. That is another instance of a union which has the welfare of society at heart and is attempting to find ways and means of assuring that other sections of our Canadian society are protected to the greatest possible extent.
I would suggest that generally speaking wage increases have relatively little effect on price increases. The Prime Minister made reference yesterday, and again today, to the inexcusable action of certain manufacturers in raising their prices. It had nothing to do with wage increases and nothing to do with negotiation. It merely had to do with an opportunity to boost prices by using the tax increases as an excuse. The attitude of the Prime Minister was that this action is inexcusable, and I am sure he would extend those remarks to price increases in other fields as well.
We know that our corporate structure in Canada, and indeed in other parts of the world, has been for quite a number of years

The Budget-Mr. Howard now developing more and more toward a monopoly or oligopoly position. More and more throughout this century there have been arrangements between companies within a nation with regard to fixing prices, the automatic raising of prices, the reducing of production and the records in the combines investigation branch of the Department of Justice are full of different practices which have been studied by the restrictive trade practices commission. More and more international cartels have been established to carve up the world into markets and assure that the highest possible income will accrue to those cartels.
We have been moving toward bigger and bigger industries, more and more price fixing arrangements, and control over our economy by outside forces. International cartels do not exist in a legal or corporate sense. In many instances they exist only by gentlemen's agreements or even by written contractual agreements, and the position is such that it is impossible for a nation to take any corrective measures to ensure that the consumer gets the fullest possible benefit from the goods produced by those particular industries.
This is one of the fields to which we should be directing a great deal of thought, as to how our Canadian governmental agencies can effectively deal with the steadily increasing cost of living and the increasing prices of goods and commodities, rather than following this blind lead which has been given to us that the unions and their members and working class people generally are entirely to blame for every price increase which takes place.
I am not in any way trying to say that unions are lily white and pure in every sense.
But unless and until the government undertakes to move in this direction and considers the necessity of instituting statutes and regulations to ensure that the consumers of Canada get the best possible deal they can in terms of price, quality of goods produced and services offered, we will continue to have the control of our society, our industry and our very economy resting in the hands of people not responsible to parliament or to the government. This government will be most derelict in its duty if it does not move in this direction.
In the speech from the throne it was indicated that changes are proposed in the combines investigation laws some time during the present session. I sincerely hope these problems are taken into consideration when this legislation is drafted, so the authorities within the combines investigation branch will be able to deal with them in a most effective way. But as long as we continue to allow the

control of our economy to rest in hands not responsible to the government, to parliament and to Canadian citizens, we will continue to be caught concurrently in depressions, inflation and out and out thievery from the pockets of the people of Canada.
Perhaps I can sum up very briefly by saying this. During the debate on the budget which was presented last year I was able to develop an anagram on the letters of the last name of the Minister of Finance. It was quite appropriate, but this particular budget does not allow me to use the last letters of the minister's name. I must therefore content myself with his initials, which I think are most appropriate, and declare the budget to be distasteful, mean and foolish.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to make a brief contribution to this debate I should like to draw your attention and that of the house to a trend which has been very noticeable in this country, and probably in every country, over the years. In the last three quarters of a century the place of government generally in the lives of Canadians and in the economy of the country has become very much greater than it used to be. For example, there are many emanations in the administrative field, and many departments, whose annual budget is now much greater than was the total budget of the federal government in the days of our grandfathers.
This is not due entirely to the development of the country and the increase which has taken place in the population, because the per capita importance of government has increased tremendously in the same period of time. During the last few years the per capita expenditure of the dominion government has been in the neighbourhood of $300 annually, whereas 75 years ago it was only $7 or $8 per capita. So it can clearly be seen that the impact of government policy, be it good or bad, is bound to have a much greater effect on the economy of the country in this day and age than it had in the days of our grandfathers.
As a matter of fact this trend has been increasing with the passing of time. In the years since 1945 the total expenditures of all governments at all levels in this country has increased by about 96 per cent. This is understandable, because governments at all levels offer a great number of services, welfare payments and projects of infinite variety which were never offered in the days of our grandfathers; some of them, indeed, could not even have existed. For example, the annual budget of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation today is much greater than the total national budget was in the days of Sir John

A. Macdonald in the last years of the nineteenth century. Thus it should readily be realized that the role of government in the everyday life of the average citizen is much greater than it used to be.
In addition to the facts I have just mentioned we are, of course, in this era of cold war faced with the necessity for spending vast amounts of money and effort on defence. There are generous payments made to other levels of government, on a scale which was unequalled in former years. The increased importance of government, with its correspondingly greater effect on the economic forces of the country means that the responsibilities which rest on any present-day government in the economic field are much greater than they used to be.
With due deference to economists, trained experts and self-appointed experts, the business of predicting the effect of any particular policy on the economy of a country is far from being an exact science, and one of the notable things about any measures which are taken is that there is a considerable time lag, usually between a year and a year and a half, between treatment and recovery.
In this connection I am struck, as a former pilot, by the close analogy between this and flying an aircraft with primary instruments. The thing that has to be learned is that when a trend shows, even to the slightest degree, corrective action must be taken early. If a trend develops, the tendency is to overcorrect when the full impact of the trend becomes apparent. We have heard repeated references in this house to unemployment. Unemployment is an unfortunate thing and is a matter of serious consequence in our economy. Nevertheless it must be realized that after the treatment is applied some time is necessary before the effects begin to appear.
There is another analogy which occurs to me from the medical field, when repeated demands arise for this or that cure in a certain situation. We do not want to be in the position of the relatives of a patient who would insist, when that patient was very ill with pneumonia, that he be given doses of penicillin every five minutes because he did not appear to be recovering. There has to be time for the treatment to take effect. In this day and age foresight is of prime importance.
When this government came to power, it found immediately that there were evidences, and sometimes danger signs, of unsatisfactory trends as far as the economy of the country was concerned. There was the prospect, the forecast, of sharply increased unemployment. There was inadequate social security, and the country was faced with a considerable decline in home building, a slowing up of the
17, 1959
The Budget-Hon. J. A. MacLean growth in personal income, an increasing disparity in the standards of government services as between provinces, increasing stocks of agricultural surpluses and many other indications of difficulties ahead.
This government acted quickly to apply treatment to some of these unsatisfactory trends. One of the earliest things it did was to stimulate home building in order to provide not only homes for Canadians but also jobs for those who build them and for the service industries which supply all the innumerable things which go into a modern home, its furnishing as well as its construction. The result was that after a decline of 8 per cent in 1957, expenditures on home building in this country rose in 1958 to $353 million or 25 per cent.
The government expanded its own capital expenditure in order to stimulate the economy and provide jobs. In addition, in co-operation with the provinces, it embarked on various projects designed to create employment quickly in certain fields, and last winter it embarked on a policy in co-operation with the provinces which allowed the municipalities to put in hand essential public works projects which, in addition to being beneficial in themselves, did at the same time provide employment for thousands of people. It will be remembered, too, that this government on coming into office immediately increased old age pensions, disabled persons' pensions, veterans' pensions and many other social benefits, besides extending hospital insurance programs to the provinces. Perhaps most important of all, it reduced taxes to those in the low income group. It increased payments to the provinces, with special adjustment grants to the Atlantic provinces, to go some considerable way, as I have already mentioned, toward eliminating the disparity between the levels of services which those provinces are able to offer as compared with most other provinces in the country.
The transfer payments of the federal government to other levels of government increased in 1958 over 1956 by $177 million. This government also placed restrictions on some types of farm products which were coming into Canada at depressed prices and glutting our own markets for Canadian producers. The government also embarked on a vigorous program of wheat sales, with the result that the wheat surplus has been cut to some extent.
In the present budget the government took further action to better the position of the Canadian farmer in his own markets by imposing reasonable duties on fruit and vegetables coming into this country, including potatoes. I am very pleased indeed to see

The Budget-Hon. J. A. MacLean this come into effect because for many years my own province, where the growing of potatoes is vitally important, was in the position of having its potatoes go into its chief market, the United States, over a duty of 37J cents per hundredweight whereas for many years United States potatoes came into Canadian markets duty free for most of the year. Two or three years ago a change was made to increase the length of time during which the duty was payable, but the present action by the government puts the Canadian producer on an even footing with his United States counterpart as far as entry into each other's market is concerned.
What are the effects of some of these policies that have been applied? I believe all Canadians are pleased to realize that during the last couple of months-for the first time in approximately 18 months, I believe- the level of unemployment is less than it was 12 months previously. There are other encouraging trends, too. Home building, which declined in 1957, rose by 25 per cent in 1958, in which year there were 164,000 starts made to establish an all-time record by 26,000 units. Net farm income, which went into a rather sharp decline in 1957, rose in 1958 by $234 million, or 24 per cent. Cash farm income rose by 8 per cent. When it is realized that the number of people engaged in agriculture declined during the same period and has been declining for many years, it will be appreciated that in 1958 the per capita cash income of people engaged in agriculture established an all-time record. The gross national product in 1958 as compared with the previous year rose by $778 million. Unincorporated non-farm business income rose by 7 per cent in 1958.
These policies which the government embarked upon were not, of course, without cost. Anyone who imagines that services and benefits can be created out of thin air is deceiving himself or the public, or both. In a rich country such as ours it is my belief and that of the government that investment in Canada and in the welfare of Canadians is money well spent. No wise government, with the conditions which have existed over the last few months would, I believe, have attempted to balance the budget, because under those circumstances such a balance would not be in the public interest.
The past year was a period when the economy of the country needed stimulation. It received that stimulation and is now responding. With the increased tempo of the economy generally it was reasonable then, to make a small increase in taxes-and it

is a relatively small increase-affecting those who are best able to carry the load. I should like to point out here and now that the income taxes paid by the low income groups in Canada, representing approximately four-fifths of the income taxpayers, have not been raised on this occasion. The income taxes paid by a vast number of Canadians are still lower than they were two years ago.
It was felt that with a gradually brightening situation steps should be taken to bring the budget more nearly into balance. That is what has been done. Those who would cry ruin because for a short period deficits have been shown are not realistic. It must be remembered that the ability of a country to carry its debt is made up of many factors. To begin with, the per capita debt of Canada is much lower at this time than it has been for long periods in the past. The development of our country, which brings our whole economy more into balance and thereby renders it able to carry with ease tax burdens which would have been completely unsupportable 40 or 50 years ago, is another consideration.
I have great confidence in our country's future. We are rich in natural resources and are blessed with one of the finest collections of racial stock that exists on the face of the earth. We live in the temperate zone in the northern regions of the world, regions which since the dawn of history have produced the greatest stimulation to human endeavour. I am convinced that Canadians in all walks of life can look forward with great confidence and optimism not only to their own immediate future but to the future of their children and their children's children.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the budget debate, I would have liked to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on last week's budget speech. Unfortunately, I am unable to do so under the circumstances, and instead I would like to tender a message of sympathy. I sympathize with the Minister of Finance for having had to bring down last week's budget. He was obliged to meet the inconsiderate expenses made during the session between the last two general elections. As a matter of fact, during that session, the Minister of Finance had to meet the expenses resulting from inconsiderate promises made during the 1957 elections and, Mr. Speaker, people in Canada now realize that they have to pay for alleged gifts.

This reminds me of a particular fact. When the present Minister of Finance was sitting in the opposition, and the Liberal government had increased the price of postage stamps by one cent after the 1953 general election, he stated, as can be seen on page 1132 of Hansard, volume II, "The chickens are coming home . .
(Text):
-the chickens are coming home to roost-
(Translation):
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the chickens are coming home to roost. We must today pay the piper, and that is what the Minister of Finance had to do last week.
When the Minister of Finance entered this house last week, I was reminded somehow of the prodigal son. The Canadian people had entrusted the Conservative party with the government of this country. The Liberal party, which had preceded the Conservative administration had left well-filled coffers. The Minister of Finance and the Conservative government have spent our legacy and today, the Minister of Finance comes back to us smiling, but empty handed, and asks us to fill his pockets again.
Mr. Speaker, the honeymoon is over. The Canadian people, which has allowed itself to be taken in by the Conservative party, now realizes, on its return from the honeymoon trip, that the magnificent engagement ring which it had been given is not even paid for. The Canadian people also have noticed that the magnificent house which had been held out as their future home was only a mirage and that the vision of stable employment at all times does not exist.
Mr. Speaker, the present government also reminds me of those used cars we buy in garages. When a buyer appears, the salesman points out the good features of the car, makes him look at all the chrome fittings, and, once the sale is made, the buyer soon realizes he is stuck with a "lemon".
Well, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people are now stuck with a "lemon", the Conservative government.
Mr. Speaker, this budget reminds me of the man standing on the highway between Ottawa and Montreal waiting for the bus to go to Montreal. After many hours, he sees a bus coming at last. He waves to the driver to stop and gets into the bus. After a while, he notices that the bus driver takes all possible roads without seeming to know exactly where he is going. The fellow gets up and asks the conductor: "Where are we going?" and the conductor replies: "But, sir, don't you know this bus is not going anywhere in
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau particular?" Well, Mr. Speaker, this government gives us the same impression, the feeling that it is not going anywhere.
Mr. Speaker, as I said just now, the honeymoon is over. Today, the government is facing the people, but the encounter is not the same as the one we saw last week on television.
At this stage of my remarks, I address my remarks particularly to the hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), and I should like to refer to this matter incidentally, because it comes under parliament and has to do with programs put on the national network of television, for which Canadians are paying the bills.
On April 12 last, at 10.30 p.m., we were given a program entitled "Aifrontement" (Encounter) which was nothing of the sort. In fact, before coming to the house this morning, I took the trouble of looking up in the Larousse the exact definition of the word "affrontement". Well, according to the dictionary, "affrontement", means "action d'af-fronter". Now, "affronter" means "to attack with intrepidity, to brave". You should have seen, Mr. Speaker, with what intrepidity the provincial member for Jeanne-Mance, Mr. Maurice Custaud, and Mr. Julien Morissette, a well-known supporter of the Union Nationale, were facing each other. Incidentally, the provincial member for Jeanne-Mance is a member of the Union Nationale and one of the parliamentary secretaries of the Union Nationale government. By the way, may I inform the house that the Union Nationale government has appointed parliamentary secretaries, which must arouse the envy of many backbenchers in this house, many of whom just now are perspiring, pining, hoping and hankering after the position of parliamentary secretary in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, it should be noted that on that program there was no actual encounter of participants. All it amounted to was fulsome praise of the Quebec government. If such programs are to be continued, in spite of protests from the people of the province of Quebec, it would be a good idea to retitle the program "Thwacks with handkerchiefs".

On the third telecast, the panelists could be the hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska (Mr. Van Horne) and Mrs. Gil-berte Cote-Mercier; they could deal with complete tax exemption in Canada. This would no doubt please the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who is obliged to tax the Canadian people.
Again on the program "Affrontement" if it should be decided to retain that name, I suggest that the panelists on the fourth telecast could be the Minister of Finance and the Canadian taxpayers. Following the budget which was introduced by the minister, we would certainly witness a real encounter.
Instead of taking pleasure in just sitting on the government benches and instead of showing smug smiles of satisfaction, members of the cabinet should endeavour to listen to the complaints of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, last Monday, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) said that he was glad that he did not have to sit any more in front of the opposition. He also added that since he was seated further from the opposition, he was closer to the people. May I advise him to be careful, for the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), in his vision, perhaps has felt that the hon. member for Sherbrooke would not stay long in this house and has placed him closer to the exit, as the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) said yesterday.
If the hon. member for Sherbrooke would get closer to the people, he would see that the people of Canada are suffering and he would hear them protesting loudly against the heavy burden of taxes they now have to bear.
Mr. Speaker, is there a more revolting sight than to see the men who now occupy the government benches-those who, for years, have been criticizing and saying that the people were too heavily taxed-unduly tax the Canadian people? When they were in the opposition, they used to tell us that taxes were too high in Canada, and now that they govern the country, they increase those taxes.
At the time they were in the opposition, they used to tell us that there was too much taxation in Canada; and now that they are in power, they tax us some more.
Mr. Speaker, during the last two election campaigns, the hon. ministers and the members who sit on the government side of the house, like the juvenile heads, the "wonder boys" they wanted to be, roved all over Canada promising tax cuts, lower expenditure, a lowering of the national debt and full employment everywhere in the country. Let me refer to only a few of the promises made by the leader of the Conservative party, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), in Toronto on April 25, 1957. This is what the Prime Minister said on that occasion, and I quote from the Montreal Star of April 26, 1957:
(Text):
It is time to take the unrepentant tax-masters off the backs of the Canadian people. No one can deny that present rates of taxation penalize success, neutralize incentive and diminish production.

Canada's present financial position is the result of a lack of administrative judgment on the part of the government, of its lack of administrative foresight and its policy of indifference and neglect.
During the campaigns which preceded the election of this parliament, the people of Canada had been promised new records of achievement. We had been promised a racing car that would take us to the highest peaks and records. But all we have now is a stock-car, headed for disaster. We do hold records, but of the wrong kind, for instance the record of unemployment, the record for peacetime government expenditure, the record for peacetime taxation, and the record for peacetime increase in the national debt. We also hold the record for peacetime deficit.
Yesterday I was listening to the speech made in this house by the member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Keays), in which he stated that at the Canadian mining convention he had met manufacturers who said to him, and I quote from page 2778 of yesterday's Hansard:
He admitted that everyone was surprised that when the experts on administration and financial affairs spoke, every one of them said there was no other course to follow and that they endorsed the courage of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming).
Well, to disprove that statement of the member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine I need only quote from the Northern Miner of February 19, 1959:
(Text):
The continuation of big deficits at Ottawa, knocking bond values down to a level that creates interest rates that stifle new capital-raising; the tax pinch on provinces and municipalities forcing them to curtail improvements; a high-cost economy that scares away foreign capital that has had so much to do with Canada's recent boom; constantly recurring big gobs of unemployment requir-

ing expensive relief; all these are plain signs that the Canadian people should stop, look and investigate.

And yet, at the same time, during the same month, the British government managed to reduce taxes while budgeting for a surplus. This government, through its leader the present Prime Minister, always a great admirer of anything British or coming from the Commonwealth, should have come to some understanding with the ministers when he was drawing up this year's budget. He should have followed the pattern set by England for the management of the people's money and, instead of a deficit budget involving tax increases, he should have announced a surplus budget with no increase in taxes.
This year's budget, Mr. Speaker, is an anti-family budget. In support of this statement, let me quote from an article in Le Devoir of Saturday April 11, 1959, under the by-line of Paul Sauriol:
-our income tax does not make sufficient allowance for essential family expenditures.
The budget submitted last week by the Minister of Finance weighs especially upon small Canadian families. The Conservative party which has always been the party of big business, was again unmindful in its budget this year of those who toil or suffer.
Last night, in his speech, the hon. member for the Magdalen Islands (Mr. Keays) gave a striking illustration of the Conservative approach when he recalled how the Prime Minister last year in Winnipeg had 

urged workers and especially the National Labour Council not to press for higher wages. The member for the Magdalen Islands said last night that higher wages would hurt corporate profits and that it was important to make sure in the first place that corporations operate at a profit before workers' wages are allowed to go up.
Mr. Speaker, after hearing those words of the member for the Magdalen Islands, I wondered about his background. I looked up the current edition of the Parliamentary Guide and I realized why the hon. member had spoken in that vein.

Mr. Speaker, as I said, this is the stand which has always been taken by the Conservative party, protect big business and forget about the workers and the small Canadian families.
As for the Liberal party, when it held power and managed the public funds, it always tried to protect the average Canadian, the worker, the ordinary people, the small wage earner. The Liberal party, through its social legislation which benefits everyone in Canada, enacted legislation such as the Family Allowances Act, the Disabled Persons Act, the Old Age Pension Act, and all the other welfare legislation which is part of the Canadian pattern.

We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a settlement of these problems not in the

spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by the present government, but in the spirit of unity and amity and with mutual tolerance and respect. (Translation):
I have here a report of the newspaper Le Soleil, dated April 30, 1957, dealing with a statement made in Charlottetown by the Prime Minister on April 29, 1957, and I quote:
During a speech in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island's capital, Mr. Diefenbaker promised that, if he should be entrusted with federal authority, he would immediately call a conference for the redistribution of fields of taxation.
Maybe that was another fleeting vision of the Prime Minister's. The present government is nothing but a government by postponement. The government has not achieved anything in the field of federal-provincial relations. It does not wish to solve that problem for fear of having to face it. Tax relations between the provinces and the central government are the best proof of this government being a government by postponement. During the 1957 pre-electoral campaign the present Prime Minister promised, if he was called upon to lead parliament, to convene a federal-provincial conference as early as September 1957. The leader of the Conservative party became Prime Minister, but he has called no such conference; he found excuses for not convening it in September. The conference took place in November 1957, in the shape of a preliminary conference to another conference which he had promised for 1958.
Everybody knows that this conference was never called.
And now, Mr. Speaker, there is talk of calling a conference of provincial treasurers, not for the purpose of settling fiscal problems but to draft a research plan which could be put into effect by a committee of officials.
Yet in 1957, the premiers of the provinces had made concrete suggestions. Why should the provincial premiers meet in Ottawa, if it is to set up a committee of officials to study those problems? In my opinion, the establishment of such a commission is useless.
As I said a moment ago, the provinces, Ontario and Manitoba particularly, made concrete suggestions during the 1957 federal-provincial conference. I feel that the federal government has had plenty of time to study those proposals, and that it should now make its intentions known to parliament, to the provinces and to the Canadian people at large.
The provinces of Ontario and Manitoba, together with the other provinces with the possible exception of Quebec, suggested to the federal government the 15-15-50 formula, which provided a deduction of 15 per cent from the individual income tax collected by the
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau provinces, of 15 per cent from the corporation income tax also collected by the provinces, and 50 per cent from the succession duties levied by the provinces.
Why does this government persist in its refusal to tell us that it is ready to accept that formula? As I said just now, there is hardly any need for a survey by officials to determine whether the federal government has the financial means to accept provincial requests and to carry out their suggestions.
Mr. Speaker, I think and I am even firmly convinced, that federalism is the only possible system in Canada. Federalism should comprise several states. We now have in this country, under our federal system, eleven states, with ten provincial governments and a central government, which means that several of those states could make some compromise, as there is a distribution of legislative power and of fiscal power.
If the federal system is essential to the Canadian nation, it has also some drawbacks which must be accepted, including some necessary compromise arrangements in the taxation field, and those arrangements should be periodically adjusted to meet economic changes in this country.
In 1955, the Liberal government and the provinces jointly found a formula which, at that time, was the best and most likely to rally all parties. I admit that the formula might be improved in the light of new needs that are now felt. In order to do this, a federal-provincial conference should be called as soon as possible in order to settle the significant matter of federal-provincial relations.
Should a federal-provincial conference be held, another matter could be dealt with, in my opinion, and it is that of indirect taxation.
As you know, under the constitution, only the federal government has a right to levy indirect taxes. And, as Mr. Duplessis, premier of Quebec, would say the provinces, all over the country, I believe, have encroached to some extent upon the field of indirect taxation. To levy indirect taxes the provinces have entrusted to the retailers, in many cases, the function of levying taxes on behalf of the provincial government. In my opinion, this is only an expedient, and the whole field of indirect taxation should be open to the provinces.
If the provinces used that method of taxation, sincerely and honestly, they could benefit from several advantages, of which the most important would be, in my opinion, the decentralization of indirect taxation, without creating any geographic inequality.

The Budget-Mr. Rouleau
Furthermore, the revenue accruing from indirect taxation does not depend so much on the industrial picture as do corporate taxes and succession duties.
The revenue from indirect taxation is more stable and, finally, the cost of its levying is lower than that of direct taxation.
At the federal-provincial conference on reconstruction, in 1945-1946, the federal government proposed to the provinces to open to them the field of indirect taxation.
At the 1950 conference, the provinces made the same suggestion, except, of course, the province of Quebec, who was opposed to it.
After the 1950 conference, the federal government circulated to the various provincial governments a proposed amendment to the constitution, which would have allowed the provinces to levy indirect taxes. However, in the face of Quebec's continued objection, the proposals were dropped. The time has come, it seems to me, for the federal government to call a federal-provincial conference, in order to find out if the province of Quebec's attitude has changed since then in that respect. However, I can see that, in the light of past experience, the federal government may well wonder whether the province of Quebec is really willing to make suggestions.
Mr. Speaker, when the member for Sherbrooke spoke in this house last Monday, he closed his remarks on education by expressing the wish that the province of Quebec take the trouble to offer definite, appropriate and constructive suggestions and proposals to the federal government. I would have liked him to enlarge upon his conclusions and to add that he wished the government of the province of Quebec would make definite and constructive suggestions and proposals to the central government in the matter of taxation.
After reading the proceedings of the federal-provincial conferences which have taken place in Ottawa, it is difficult, I know, to expect that the premier of Quebec will offer anything else but beautiful sentences. He will probably never submit definite proposals.
Mr. Duplessis' speech to the December 1950 conference, may be summarized by the paragraph appearing on page 27 of the proceedings. I quote:
(Text):
Co-operation is not centralization; co-operation is not assimilation; co-operation is not bureaucracy;
[Mr. Eouleau-1

co-operation is the friendly and mutual collaboration of two fellow Canadians working loyally hand in hand respecting fully the rights of each other, so as to safeguard and stabilize the future of Canada by rendering full justice to each and every one.
(Translation) :
Such is the purport of the speeches made by the premier of the province of Quebec.
