subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising at this time to make my contribution to the budget debate I should like first of all to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for the excellent manner in which he presented the budget to the House of Commons. The manner in which it was presented shows that he devoted much study and hard work to it and no doubt he consulted and sought the advice of experts in every phase of the economy before arriving at his final decision.
The opposition have been taking the same approach as last year, clouding and casting smoke screens over all the issues. They take delight in citing past statements of the Minister of Finance and other hon. members of the government. I should like to remind hon. members of the opposition that some of the statements made by them last year in the budget debate make funny reading today.
I do not profess to be an expert on matters of finance but I believe I have the average good sense and show the same responsibility of duty as the average Canadian. The average Canadian has accepted this budget. Last year the Minister of Finance predicted an increase of 2 per cent in our national production. Opposition members made fun of this and said that he was being highly optimistic. They also tried to make fun of the large deficit forecast a year ago. After listening to them for many days one got the impression they were secretly hoping conditions would get worse and not better. I honestly think they were disappointed when the white paper was presented to the house on April 8 showing that our total national production has increased by 2J per cent and that the deficit was considerably less than forecast. Even though this did not please the opposition I am sure it pleased the people of Canada.
In my opinion the Minister of Finance and the government deserve much credit for checking the two evils they inherited from the former government, unemployment and inflation. The opposition have now embarked on the same line of criticism they adopted

The Budget-Mr. Stefanson last year and one again gets the impression that they hope things will worsen and not improve. The people of Canada have every reason to have confidence in the predictions of the Minister of Finance for the coming year. All they have to do is take as a guide the predictions of a year ago in which he forecast conditions so accurately.
This year the minister has forecast an increase of 7 per cent in our national production and a budget deficit of $393 million. I am confident that at the end of the year both these figures will be bettered; that is to say, the gross national product will be more than 7 per cent higher and the deficit will be less than estimated. In some press reports this has been termed a recovery budget. I believe the words of the minister as reported at page 2425 of Hansard of April 9, are worthy of repetition. During the course of his budget speech the minister said:
Just as last year's budget was designed to meet 1958 economic conditions and needs, so this year's budget is designed to meet the changed conditions and needs of 1959. In a period when economic conditions are undergoing rapid change, our approach to our fiscal problems must be flexible and adaptable.
This budget has been designed to foster and promote recovery. Our aim is to maintain a sustainable rate of growth in terms of employment, development of resources and a sound dollar, so that Canadians everywhere may find full expression for their enterprise, industry and aspirations as free men and women.
Canada has no reason for fear. Blessed as she has been by a benign Providence above all other lands, she can face her shining future with utmost confidence.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that I am not happy about increases in taxes and I am sure that none of our people are. In this we no doubt agree wholeheartedly. However, my hon. friends to my right are not altogether correct or fair in their criticism when they say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and other members of the government had promised tax cuts and increased social services. Members of the government did promise tax cuts in the campaign prior to the June 10 election and they did fulfil those promises when they introduced the baby budget of 1957 which lowered taxes and increased social services. They definitely kept faith with the people of Canada. However, when they assumed office they did not fully realize how bad the situation was, nor did they have all the facts. When they took office they became aware of conditions in the country brought about by the policies of the former government and became aware of the extent to which unemployment and inflation prevailed. The last budget brought in by the former government helped to aggravate both these conditions.

Last year's deficit budget represented a remedial step to help check both the evils mentioned and the actions of this government have helped to bring about a steady recovery.
My friend the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Keays) in his remarks quoted a statement made by Mr. A. C. Ashford, president of the Canadian chamber of commerce, which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, and I wish now to make reference to a statement by Mr. Ashford reported in the Winnipeg Tribune of April 10. I am a member of a small chamber of commerce and through my association with the Canadian chamber of commerce I have found them to be sound in their judgment on most matters. The article reads as follows:
A. C. Ashford, president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, told the Tribune today a more balanced budget means general business improvement but that high taxation can be harmful on a long term basis for a young developing country like Canada. He said, "I believe a balanced budget, or close to one, would improve the bond market and general business. I personally was not surprised at the increase in income taxes to meet the current situation. However. I do feel that income taxes are too high on a long term basis for a young developing country like Canada.
We cannot expect the government to lower taxes if we, the public, are constantly asking them to do more and more for us. Every penny the government spends has to come out of the pocket of the taxpayers. There is no other source. I am pleased to see the Minister of Finance is optimistic about the volume of this year's business."
Mr. Ashford, incidentally, is also president of the Toronto-Dominion Bank. The Ottawa Citizen on April 13, under the heading, "Budget Hikes Necessary, Realtor Says", carried another interesting article which reads as follows:
Donald H. Koyl of Saskatoon, president of the Canadian association of real estate boards, says recent tax increases announced in the federal budget were necessary.
Mr. Koyl, here to attend the B.C. association of real estate boards convention, said the budget was not inflationary. It was foolish for a government to do heavy deficit financing when it could be avoided and an increase in taxes was not inflationary.
Mr. Koyl then went on to say that the real estate business in Canada is in a very sound condition.
This budget was designed to bring about a further recovery. No matter how much we dislike higher taxes they are necessary to meet higher national bills and to keep our dollar sound. Over half the increase in taxes goes toward the old age security fund to put it on a sound basis for the first time. Since the fund was set up and a formula adopted it has always operated in the red. I am sure that every Canadian is glad to

see this fund put on a sound basis. I am sure that no one would want to see the old age pension decreased.
I personally believe that many of our senior citizens are having difficulties in getting by on the present pension. I do feel that we should give serious consideration to increasing the pension for needy pensioners as well as to lowering the age limit. In my home town of Gimli, Manitoba we have the Betel old folks' home, one of the finest establishments of this nature in Canada. Any community contemplating building a senior citizen's home, no doubt could get valuable information from the board of directors of this institution.
No doubt what annoys the members of the opposition is that the public have accepted this budget and have accepted the tax increases as necessary. They realize that they are getting far greater social service benefits than ever before and that these things have to be paid for. No one wants smaller old age pensions, smaller family allowances, smaller pensions for the blind, smaller veterans' pensions and so on. Mr. Speaker, if the public were asked to vote on these services I am sure it would vote overwhelmingly in favour of maintaining them. Furthermore, the hospital plan has come into operation since this government took office and this creates a large expenditure of money. This is another matter that the people approve of.
Another large item of expense is for national defence, and I have not heard the opposition suggest that this is not necessary. With present world conditions and the cold war, this expenditure appears absolutely necessary. It is also spread throughout the country and does help the economy of the country. In Gimli we have an R.C.A.F. station, and its location there has given considerable employment to people living in the vicinity. I am sure that the people in that area want to see that air force station remain there in operation indefinitely.
Last year in my maiden speech I gave a brief outline of the boundaries of my constituency and also a brief description of the people and their occupations. When you look at the map of Canada you can see that Manitoba is the centre of Canada and is known as the keystone province. The centre of Manitoba is the interlake area which comprises the constituency of Selkirk. The boundaries of the Selkirk constituency follow the east shore of lake Winnipeg and the west shore of lake Manitoba and includes all the land between those lakes, and includes both lake Winnipeg and lake Manitoba.
Most of the people of my constituency are primary producers. They are engaged either in farming or fishing. Generally, people who
The Budget-Mr. Stefanson are primary producers are proud and independent. This is true of all the people in my constituency. They greatly value their freedom and the opportunities of earning a livelihood through their own efforts. They are not the type that expect handouts from the government. These people have worked hard, and it is throughout all this area that we have the real, genuine family farms. The interlake area is sometimes referred to as the breadbasket of Manitoba. There have been times when these people have met with hardships through drought and flooding. When people are faced with such conditions through no fault of their own the government should assist.
This government since coming into office has introduced legislation and has an agricultural program tailored to meet the needs of the farmers. Since taking office this government has introduced the stabilization act, paid cash advances on grain, made acreage payments and amended the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to the point where it is now much more practical and much more acceptable to the farmers.
This year in the throne speech the government indicated that it will be bringing in legislation dealing with crop insurance and farm credit. Legislation regarding farm credit will be of real benefit to the farmers. I think all of this legislation has been asked for by farm organizations, and all of it is aimed at improving the conditions of those engaged in agriculture. I feel confident that this government will continue to study the problems of agriculture and when necessary bring in legislation accordingly.
The fishermen in my constituency have also had good years and bad years. Some years the fish just do not seem to be there. Nobody knows the reason why. Recently in my province the fishermen formed the Manitoba federation of fishermen, and they have already met with the government of that province to discuss the industry. There is real need for some form of credit system for fishermen. At present the only credit available is from the fish companies, and I am sure they would be glad to get out of this financing. There is need for more research and also a need for better advertising, and an education program on the cooking and the preparation of fish. There is no problem in selling certain fish and it brings a high price on the export market. Pickerel, white fish, sauger, perch and goldeye are among these. It is for what we call the rough fish that such a publicity and educational campaign is required.
I have mentioned briefly some of the problems of the farmer and the fisherman. I also wish to point out that the increase in

The Budget-Mr. Stefanson income tax and corporation tax affects very few people in my constituency.
I pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that Manitoba is the centre of the nation and the Selkirk constituency is the centre of Manitoba. It is like the core of the nation. Take the core of an apple; when the core is healthy the rest of the apple is also generally healthy. Manitoba is the core of the nation and that core is in excellent condition; therefore the rest of the nation is also healthy.
Manitoba is blessed with having an excellent government. Mr. Roblin and his colleagues are giving the province real progressive legislation, and I am sure the people of Manitoba will show their appreciation of this at the polls on May 14.
Recently, a report released by the retail merchants' association in Manitoba showed a large increase in retail sales. This shows conditions in the country to be the direct opposite of what opposition members are preaching.
The government of the province of Manitoba tackles the problems before them and does something about them. The education bill is an example, and I could give the house many more. The attitude of the previous government was, "we will wait and see".
I am pleased to see that the grants to the provinces are higher than at any time before and almost double those of three years ago. With the grants to the provinces larger, they in turn can make larger grants to the municipalities, which have a very limited income through the real estate tax. The services that municipalities are being called on today to supply cannot be financed through the real estate tax, and their only other source of income is government grants.
This morning the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) outlined very well that the budgets of all forms of government, municipal, provincial, et cetera have greatly increased during the past years, and the services being rendered have increased many times over what they were 50 years ago.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten), as reported at page 2773 of Hansard, last night referred to the meeting that the Prime Minister held in Selkirk. He said:
The Prime Minister went on to speak in Selkirk, Manitoba, on March 7,-
That is an error; it should be March 17.
-1958, as reported in the Toronto Telegram of March 18. After claiming that the government had eased the tight money situation, he went on to say:
"This has been done by releasing $300 million for new housing, launching a vast public works program and by reducing taxes."
Incidentally, I wonder where that public works program went to.


Of course, he must admit that the housing program has been a huge success and that we built more houses last year than at any time before. When I went home at Easter I was amazed to see the number of new houses being put up in the town of Selkirk during the past winter and being constructed at the present time.
As far as the public works program is concerned, I am also aware of some of that work being done, as this government has been participating in the cost of roads being built along the west shore of lake Winnipeg on a 50-50 basis with the provinces. They have also just recently given out contracts for three extensions to wharves in my constituency. I can assure you that this public works program is going on, and I can refer also to several public buildings for which contracts have been awarded or which tenders for construction are being called for.
Before I conclude my remarks there are a few things that I want to mention briefly that are of real importance to the people of my constituency. One thing that is badly needed is improved television. I am continually getting complaints, petitions and so forth from the people of the interlake area requesting television facilities. If the C.B.C. is not prepared to give these facilities, then serious consideration should be given to granting a licence to a private station that would be willing to render this service.
Another thing that is of importance to my riding is northern development. Roads and communication are of real importance to such development. The development of our natural resources is very important, and to accomplish this one has to build railroads, highways and communication systems into these areas. In the Arthur D. Little report on the economy of Manitoba it is proposed that a railroad be constructed from Gypsumville to Grand Rapids and to Wekusko on the Hudson Bay railway. This would shorten the distance from southern Manitoba to Churchill by quite a bit. This report also points out that Grand Rapids is a logical point for a power development project on the Saskatchewan river, and if power were developed a pulp and paper mill would be built. These are sound projects and serious consideration should be given to carrying them out.
I was extremely interested in the report of the lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba board which was presented to this government last June. The board was established jointly by the federal and provincial governments. Following this report the province had the benefit of a cost analysis made of the proposed lake Manitoba regulation. The findings of this study are contained in a report entitled

"Benefit-Cost Analysis, Lake Manitoba Regulations, September, 1958". This report shows that regulation of lake Manitoba is economically feasible. I appreciate the action taken by the provincial government, and this is a project worthy of support by this government. Controlling the level of this lake will not only benefit those engaged in agriculture, but it will, I am sure, have a beneficial effect on fishing and hunting. It will also provide much better beaches.
Before I resume my seat I did want to make a further mention of northern development program. Last fall I was very much interested in hearing a lecture given in Winnipeg by the Arctic explorer Vilhjalmur Stefansson. I cannot claim to be related in any way to him. However, he was born at Arnes, which is in the Selkirk constituency. He spent many years in the Arctic. In fact, he wrote a book back in 1922, "The Northward Course of Empire." I am just paraphrasing some of the things he said in this lecture. I think it was his third Arctic expedition which was financed by the United States government. They gave him $50,000. Then, he found himself running out of money. He knew the head of some university in Ontario as well as the president of some bank, and between them they got him an appointment with the prime minister of the day, who at that time was Borden. Stefansson talked with Mr. Borden and suggested that he would like to get $25,000 from the Canadian government because any land he might discover would be north of Canada. The next day he met with Mr. Borden who had met with his cabinet and Borden told him that he was sorry but they had turned down the offer. However, Mr. Borden said, "I will tell you what we will do; we will take over the expedition." They paid back the $50,000 to the United States and Canada took over the expedition.
During the course of this expedition he discovered five large islands in the Arctic. He named all those islands after Conservative cabinet ministers. There is Brock, Lockheed, Borden and I forget some of the others. Then, he said the Liberals came into power and they referred to this as a Conservative archipelago. Then, he referred to what he thought was a sort of mean trick. Several years later when they flew over this largest island which he had named Borden it was found that what he had thought was a large bay was actually a strait, so there were two islands. Now, the Liberals were in power and they named the larger island Mackenzie King island. You can check this on the map. It was very interesting for me to hear this. He said,
The Budget-Mr. Carter referring to the book "The Northward Course of Empire", that it had finally caught on when Diefenbaker was elected; they had seen the vision of development in the north, and I am sure this development will continue steadily.
In concluding, I should like to point out that Canada is well on the road to recovery and can look forward to a steady expansion in economic activity, employment and income. The policies being pursued by the present government assure the people of Canada a bright future.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this debate occurs at a time so close to the tenth anniversary of confederation with Newfoundland one would normally use this occasion to say something about the impact which confederation has had on the tenth province. However, recent events have rendered that inadvisable, so I shall restrict my remarks to registering the keen disappointment and the utter disillusionment of the people of my province at the treatment which they have received from this government. I shall reserve further remarks until the appropriate legislation comes before this house.
Yesterday the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) dwelt at considerable length on the subject of democracy and particularly democracy as it is practised by corporations and by labour unions. Today I should like to add a few words of my own on this subject. Despite the successes which the Russians have had in perverting the meaning of words there is still only one kind of democracy, and that democracy is founded on the bedrock of the importance of the individual and the nature of the individual as a created being. The human personality has worth within himself as a human being and because of that he has certain God-given rights which should not be violated by the state, by any organization or by any other person.
Democracy also recognizes that among these fundamental rights there are priorities and the highest priority goes to the right to live. As Shylock said in "The Merchant of Venice", you take away my life when you take away from me the means to support that life. Democracy also distinguishes between God-given fundamental human rights of a human personality and the legal rights of an impersonal organization which are conferred upon it by man.
The hon. member for Port Arthur yesterday pointed his finger at corporations and observed that they were not very democratic in their actions. Then he went on to use that argument to justify the same kind of

The Budget-Mr. Carter action on the part of unions; in other words, two wrongs make a right. Naturally this raised some questions in my mind, and to balance the arguments put on Hansard yesterday by the member for Port Arthur I should like to read excerpts from two articles which appeared recently in the Newfoundland press. The first article is taken from the Evening Telegram of St. John's, Newfoundland, for February 27, 1959. It is a press report from Grand Falls by Ian Macdonald. I quote:
The Canadian Labour Congress took away the charter of the Grand Falls-Gander district labour council early today for their stand against the striking international woodworkers of America (C.L.C.). It was the first punitive action taken by the C.L.C. against any labour body as a result of the bitter and violence-spattered strike of 1,200 I.W.A. loggers against the Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company.
I skip a portion because I do not want to take up too much of Hansard with this article and I come to another excerpt from the same article which gives the meat of the problem:
Eight of the twelve unions represented at the special labour council meeting left en masse after Mr. Rhodes called on them to back the I.W.A. strike. The meeting was called to discuss the reinstatement of Sterling Thomas as council president. He was suspended as president of the 3,000-member council and as vice-president of the Newfoundland federation of labour by the Canadian Labour Congress for his opposition to I.W.A. "tactics" during the two-month strike of 1,200 loggers.
A statement issued by Mr. Grimes on behalf of the eight dissenting unions said:
"At a meeting tonight of the council with C.L.C. representatives C. W. Strong and Henry Rhodes the suspension of Sterling Thomas was discussed. After about one hour it was pointed out that the council had no alternative except to come out and file full support to the I.W.A. and notify the premier to this effect. On this statement, eight unions rose as a body and walked out of the labour council."
The second article is much shorter and comes from the St. John's Daily News of February 23, 1959. It contains a statement made by Mr. Thomas himself describing what led up to the action referred to in the article I have just read, and it reads as follows:
Sterling Thomas, ousted president of the Grand Falls and Gander district trades and labour council, has accused the Canadian Labour Congress and the Newfoundland federation of labour of taking discriminatory action against him. . . . Mr. Thomas told the Daily News he can come to no other conclusion than that he has been discriminated against in view of the fact that other affiliates of the two bodies have expressed just as strong support for Premier Smallwood's stand and no action has been taken against them. He said, "They too are governed by the regulations of the federation and C.L.C.". Mr. Thomas said he was particularly surprised at Mr. Jodoin's action in the light of the work that he, (Mr. Thomas) has done in re-organizing and helping to firmly establish the Grand Falls-Gander council. He pointed out

that over the past two years a lot of work had been done to get the council on its feet and to make it a strong member of the C.L.C. and the federation. His reward, he said, is to be thrown out without a hearing. He said, even more disturbing is the fact that even though there was a C.L.C. representative in Grand Falls he was never once approached about his stand. He was not given the opportunity to defend or explain his actions.
For the benefit of hon. members I should point out that Mr. Sterling Thomas is an officer of an international union of long standing and that he bears the highest repute in his community. The hon. member for Port Arthur is not in his seat at the moment but if he were I would naturally like to ask him if this was the kind of democracy to which he was referring yesterday.
I should like to take a few minutes now, Mr. Speaker, to deal with the budget. The purpose of any budget is to give a clear, concise picture of the state of the national health, describing what maladies may be present and what remedies are prescribed to cure them. The real test, therefore, of a budget is the clarity and accuracy with which it presents that picture. Since the budget concerns everyone it should be presented in such terms that the ordinary man in the street can understand its salient points.
The present budget follows that traditional pattern which has been established over the years and which is getting far too complicated to be understood by the man in the street. The pertinent facts are buried under masses of words, figures and graphs, buried so deeply that you have to use a pickaxe to dig them out. The present budget is perhaps a little wordier and more complicated than that of last year. The astronomical figures are beyond the ordinary man's comprehension and the very form of the budget tends to conceal important facts rather than expose them.
We can understand, of course, the human tendency to present unpleasant facts in as favourable a light as possible, particularly in a light favourable to the party in power. That is a human failing but it is one that carries with it certain disadvantages because the time has come when we must treat the Canadian taxpayer as a mature individual, one who is able to face unpleasant facts and one who has a great part to play in whatever remedies may be prescribed.
The most important fact of any budget is that there is only one pie. During elections we hear a great deal about pie in the sky. During the last two elections I think we had more pie of that kind than ever before in our history. We were told about savings of $500 million of waste and extravagance, of more spending, greater pensions, less taxes and of

course a balanced budget. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson) who has just taken his seat said, "Of course, everyone understands that these things have to be paid for". I challenge him or anybody to get on the floor and give one instance where anyone in the last two elections told the taxpayers they could have all these additional things but they had to be paid for.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I accept the challenge.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, not very many have. There was certainly nothing said about paying the bill, according to the speeches of the Conservative party spokesmen during the last two elections. I have read most of the reports both during the elections and afterwards, but I do not recall very much stress being laid on the fact that you can have more pie but you have to pay for it.
That particular kind of pie is proving very indigestible at this moment. Every new speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) described a brand new millennium that was coming to pass, and a greater and greater vision was going to be revealed according to every speaker. But nothing was ever said about the cost. Certainly as far as the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is concerned, I remember nothing being said about costs. But I can remember many occasions when the Prime Minister pointed his finger at the Liberals and said, "They said it could not be done, but give us a chance and we will show you." In the last election he said, "We did it."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did your leader do?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We never said it could not be done. What we said was it could not be done and balance the budget. This budget, of course, confirms exactly what we said. There is an old saying, "You can be sure your sins will find you out", and this budget really confirms this saying. At least, the budget admits that the piper has played, the people have danced to his tune, and now the piper has to be paid. Of course, I realize that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) implied the other day that these promises were not meant to be taken too seriously, but I do not think he advised anybody to that effect during the election. The fact is that people did take them seriously, and while one may think that the reason the people were hoodwinked was because they wanted to be hoodwinked, nevertheless they have now been forced to learn some very painful facts. The Canadian people have been told there is no pie in the sky after all. You cannot get something for nothing. Everything must be paid for soon or later; in this
The Budget-Mr. Carter case it is going to be later. No matter how you carve it up there is still only one pie and only one taxpayer.
The man in the street is concerned, I think, first and foremost about that pie. What he wants particularly to know from the budget is how big is this pie? Is it getting bigger or smaller, and what is happening to his particular share? Well, the budget is not too helpful in that respect. The budget gives the size of the pie in figures which do not mean what they say, and can be very deceiving.
I	noticed that the hon. member for Selkirk was very deceived when he made reference to it, as also was the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) this morning. If you really want to find out what is happening to the pie-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Whose figures are these?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: These figures can be verified by the dominion bureau of statistics any time you wish. If we want to find out if the gross national product is getting bigger we have to convert it into terms of constant dollars. The dollars which my hon. friend from Selkirk referred to this afternoon, and the Minister of Fisheries this morning, were 1958 dollars. That is a very different kind of animal from the 1949 dollar. Also, the increase is made up of two parts, and only one part is due to the increase in volume, which is the important thing. The other part is the increase in prices, which is a very serious thing. If you convert it to 1949 dollars you get the true picture with regard to the increase in volume. In 1954 our gross national product in ordinary dollars was $24,871 billion; it was down 0.6 per cent. But when it was converted to 1949 dollars, the volume was down 3 per cent. That is, the volume of production went down and the reason the over-all change was only 0.6 per cent was that 2.6 per cent of that was made up by increased prices; in other words, by inflation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are these your figures?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
These figures were received from the bureau of statistics and can be obtained from the library. In 1955 the gross national product was $27.07 billion, up 9 per cent; but in constant dollars it was only $21,961 billion, up 8 per cent. That was the year when we did have stable prices and very little inflation. The increase in volume was 8 per cent out of a total of 9 per cent, showing only 1 per cent inflation. In 1956 it was $30,098 billion, up
II	per cent; in constant dollars it was $23,547 billion, up only 7 per cent; in other words, 4 per cent inflation. In 1957, and this is important, the figure was $31,406 billion, up 4 per cent apparently; but in

The Budget-Mr. Carter constant dollars the figure was only $23.51 billion; in actual volume it was down 1 per cent. In 1958 it was $32,189 billion, apparently up 2J per cent; in constant dollars, $23,704 billion, up only 0.8 per cent.
These figures which I have just quoted show in terms of constant dollars that there was very little change in gross national product in the years 1956, 1957 and 1958. In fact, there was hardly any change at all. If the population had remained unchanged the size of the individual share of the pie would have been unchanged too, but during those years our population increased. In 1954 it was 15.28 million; in 1955 it was 15.69 million, up 3 per cent; in 1956 it was 16.081 million, up 2 per cent; in 1957 it was 16.589 million, up 3 per cent; in 1958 it was 17.048 million, up 2 per cent. Thus, in the three years when our gross national product was stationary, the population was steadily increasing as an average rate of 2.5 per cent per year and the size of the individual piece of pie was becoming smaller.
If we think in terms of the labour force, we see that the labour force in 1954 was 5.493 millions; in 1955 it was 5.610 millions; In 1956, 5.782 millions; in 1957, 6.003 millions; and in 1958, 6.127 millions. The increase in the labour force is a little out of line with the change in population due, of course, to immigration, but if we look at the increase which took place in the labour force and take into consideration the fact that total production was practically unchanged, it is clear that each worker during the last three years has been producing considerably less than did an individual worker in 1955.
I have these figures in the form of two tables and it might be more convenient for the house if I were given consent to place them on record in Hansard in tabular form.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Were the tables prepared by the hon. member or by the dominion bureau of statistics?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are excerpts from the d.b.s. figures.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the hon. member leave to have these two tables inserted in his speech at this point?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How have the Liberals been increasing in the last few years?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You cannot digest the ones you have at this moment. You had good Liberal pie for 22 years but you did not appreciate it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It went rotten.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, the people now have a chance to taste the difference.
Next to the gross national product, the problems which most interest the man in the street concern the twin subjects of unemployment and inflation. The effect of inflation is illustrated by the figures which I mentioned a few moments ago. The gross national product last year amounted to $32,189 billions, but this had the value of only $23,704 billion when the value of the dollar is kept at a constant figure. In other words, it takes roughly $32 now to buy what could be bought in 1949 for $23.50. The Canadian dollar has lost one-third of its value in the past ten years.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did you say "few years"?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is where the inflation was, in the last two years.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those who are in a position to do so can keep abreast of this dollar depreciation by demanding more dollars, but if they do so they make the situation even worse for those who are not in that position. Currency debasement is just as great a threat to national security as missiles are, and it is far more insidious. Obviously something needs to be done about this. Perhaps we should make a thorough inquiry into our whole monetary system, including the question of interest rates.
As far as unemployment is concerned, jobs depend mainly on two things, foreign trade and the provision of capital investment. New jobs depend on capital investment. I do not know what the actual figure is with respect to each job provided, but it is somewhere between $10,000 and $25,000. But capital investment in 1957 amounted to only $8.7 billion; in 1958 it was $8.4 billion; and in 1959, only $8.3 billion. In other words, capital investment this year is $400 million less than it was in 1957, and in 1957 our total production was 1 per cent less in volume than in 1956. How, in the face of this situation,

can the minister expect a 7 per cent increase in the gross national product next year?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will find out.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where is it coming from? I can tell the hon. member, whoever he was, that an article by Mr. E. J. DeSeau in the Financial Times dated April 11 inferred that if it takes place it must be due to inflation. If there is a better explanation we are ready to hear it, but nobody has explained it yet. The figures just do not add up to 7 per cent, or even to 4 per cent.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They do not add up to a billion dollar deficit, anyway.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, they do add up to an $800 million deficit.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some of the members in this part of the house are feeling excluded.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Look at the Speaker.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker. I was getting so much attention from that part of the house-but I certainly did not mean any disrespect to the Chair.
If we are to cure our unemployment problem it must be done by using the industrial capacity we have idle at the moment and by creating new jobs through capital investment. The figures which the minister has tabled do not indicate that nearly enough is being done in this direction, even without taking into account the natural increase in the labour force. In addition, also, we must take into consideration the effects of automation. We must remember that in the United States the pre-recession level of production was reached a short while ago but the number of workers employed was one million less than were employed prior to the recession, the difference being due to automation. We must realise that these forces are at work in Canada, and the only logical conclusion we can reach is that unemployment will continue to be a problem for some years yet.
The other point, of course, is trade. Twenty per cent of our jobs depend upon trade, and the international picture is not nearly as encouraging as the budget would seem to indicate. This is pointed out in an article in the Gazette of March 31. Referring to what it calls special items, this article says:
The maintenance of exports would have been more encouraging were it not for the influence of "special items" in which uranium shipments were foremost.
These were worth $277 million last year, compared to $128 million in 1957 and $46 million in 1956. The export of aircraft and parts, and cattle and meat, at $109 million and $153 million respectively, were double the 1957 figure.
When these "special items" are subtracted from the export total, a more realistic assessment of
The Budget-Mr. Carter
the impact of recession on the export trade is available. At $3,758 million, exports of mineral products, wood and paper products, other agriculture and fish products, and manufactured goods are $380 million less than in 1957.
This is an extract from an article written by John Meyer, financial editor of the Gazette which appeared in the March 31, issue.
The commonwealth trade and commerce conference about which we heard so much also has not turned out to be the success we were lead to believe it was, at least not in the eyes of the Tory counterparts in the United Kingdom parliament. I wish to read now from a statement made by Sir Albert Braithwaite as reported at page 1112 of the British Hansard of December 2, 1958:
First of all, I should like to pay tribute to the chancellor of the Exchequer and the president of the board of trade for the brilliance which they displayed in leading our own delegation to the Montreal Conference. Reading between the lines, it seems to me that what they did there literally saved the conference from being almost a stalemate. They infused some life into it. At the same time I am not satisfied that the conference report is by any means a document upon which to rebuild and revitalize the British commonwealth of nations. Its implications are narrow. It is phlegmatic. It is not precise enough in its conclusions, and it gives no real, positive direction on how even those conclusions will be carried out.
I wanted something much more vital to lead our commonwealth affairs than a lot of pious platitudes. Many people have said a great many things about how we should develop the commonwealth, but there has been a remarkable absence of action since the Montreal conference took place. The Canadian Prime Minister came over here and made great speeches on what should be done, but I have seen no real reflection in deeds implementing the words which he uttered.
Those words were not spoken by a Liberal or Socialist member of the British parliament but by a Conservative.
In the few moments left at my disposal I should like to deal briefly with the bond conversion. Last year the Minister of Finance came before us and told us about the problem of refinancing. He had, he said, $6.4 billion falling due in eight years which meant an average of $8 million worth of bonds falling due each year. That situation, he indicated, was likely to cause instability in the bond market during that period of time. His solution was to convert to long term bonds and spread the repayment over a longer period. That, of course, appeared to be a very sound idea. But what has actually happened? Less than half-45 per cent to be exact-of those original bonds were converted to long term bonds. Suppose we say half. The sum of $3.2 billion of original debt is still coming due within the seven year period. We must then add to that the $3.3 billion of new borrowing which has been made by this government since it came to power. I should like to emphasize that all
2812	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy of this borrowing is short term borrowing of less than three years. If we add half of the original amount, $3.2 billion, to the new borrowing of $3.3 billion-and I hope my hon. friend is checking on the mathematics at this point-we still have $6.5 billion falling due in the next eight years and so we still have the original problem with which we were faced.
If we have gained anything by that transaction I should like to have the Minister of Finance explain to us just what it is. On the other hand, we have paid a very high price for that experiment. We have to pay $340 million in extra interest on bonds maturing between 1960 and 1966. We have to add to that $31 million in premiums, bonuses, for advertising, etc. While we still have the original problem that existed before the conversion took place we also have increased our indebtedness by $345 million. I have much more to say but I think this perhaps would be a convenient time to stop.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since becoming a member of this honourable house it has not been my lot to swell the records with many words and I assure you that on this occasion I intend to continue my brevity. When I was very young I was advised that no man learns wisdom while talking and since I have been a member of this house-and I have been here some time now-I have often wondered if the same thing does not apply to listening.
I take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for the splendid budget he has presented. I do not propose to comment at length upon it, but I suggest it is one which should appeal to Canadians generally as a compromise to our economy and an incentive to all to participate in the great future which this country offers.
And now, since it is my privilege to represent the finest constituency in Canada, I should like to transgress a little on the time of the house to say a few things about my part of the country and the excellent people who live there. Geographically, the counties of Colchester and Hants are located in the centre of Nova Scotia, hinging on the town of Truro which is known as the hub of Nova Scotia. Our lands envelop the headwaters of the famous Cobequid bay and run north to a short frontage on the strait of Northumberland. It is unique that I am nearly surrounded by and border on the constituencies of seven of the other eleven members who represent Nova Scotia in this house. I assure you that it is very comforting to have such wonderful neighbours.
The good judgment of my people is well known provincially because at present we


are represented in the legislature by four members on the government side. Of these, one is deputy speaker, another is our excellent minister of highways and a third is none less than the distinguished premier of Nova Scotia.
This constituency is steeped in history and the area bordering the Cobequid bay and the north shore still bear evidence of Acadian settlement as far back as the 17th century. Because we are blessed by fertile lands bordering our shores and in our many river valleys our economy is based chiefly on agriculture which is, in most cases, coupled closely with the harvest of wood products from our forests.
The world-renowned tides of the Cobequid bay at some points and in some cases rise to heights of over 60 feet above low water, and the action of these turbulent waters entering and receding from the rivers have over the years built up large areas of fertile marsh lands. It was part of these lands that the early settlers reclaimed and tilled to support themselves and their livestock. Today, thanks to the assistance rendered by the Maritime Marshland Reclamation Act, thousands of acres of marsh lands are being turned into crop and grazing areas. The people who own those lands are very grateful for this assistance, and I hope that this program will continue to the benefit of all areas.
Owing to the steepness of the watersheds on our rivers, occasional flooding is a menace to those who live in the lower valley areas. Erosion of valuable farmland is also much in evidence. This situation has been aggravated somewhat by the removal of timber from the slopes. Owing to the intensity of this erosion and the increased cost of labour and materials, the farmers are finding it most difficult to provide necessary protection. I fully realize that this is a widespread problem, and I am happy that a study is being made to ascertain whether some assistance is warranted. There are several inland areas inundated by shallow water at the present time which could be brought under cultivation by drainage. Perhaps the provisions of the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act could be extended to include projects of upland erosion and drainage.
I have already mentioned that the cutting of timber has upset water control, and although it is generally recognized that natural rehabilitation of forests is as fast here as anywhere else in Canada, recent surveys show that growth is not keeping pace with cutting. We have learned to assist nature in our field production and I believe it is high time that we applied more common sense to forest management. Even if

we give a tree a good chance we must realize that it takes nearly a generation to produce.
Because our economy is so closely tied to the forest products industry, it is both desirable and necessary to continue limited production. Financial returns are continually diminishing and the recent increase in freight rates has dealt a very serious blow to our home markets. Mr. Speaker, I urge this administration to expedite, and quickly, a complete review of the freight rate structure, with the objective of equalization of advantage to all Canadians in all industries.
Our principal manufacturing is in the textile field located in the towns of Truro and Windsor. Good management and skilled craftsmen have combined here to produce, and even now we are expanding in the production of excellent quality goods which are famous from coast to coast. The quarrying and export of gypsum and barytes adds to the economy of a large area, as does the manufacture and export of pulp products in the western area.
Owing to our short coastline fishing is done only on a limited and seasonal scale. Because we are centrally situated transportation plays an important part in our general activity. Both railways and highway transport converge on Truro from all directions. Many hon. members of this house who were among the thousands of troops who proceeded overseas during the last war will recall Truro as the last train stop before reaching the point of embarkation. To those of you who can find time for a holiday I commend to you the excellent scenery of Cobequid, the valleys, streams and hills, and the beautiful and excellent bathing beaches of the north shore where the water temperature is most inviting. For the outdoor sportsman there are many inland waters and forests which will reward exploration during the midseasons.
I am proud to report that the general economy of my constituency has held fairly firm, and many indications point to a steady improvement. This speaks well for the people who are resourceful and believe in steady progress. Those people believe in keeping one foot on the ground and consolidating each step rather than getting up in the air and expecting someone else to come to their rescue.
Problems, Mr. Speaker! Certainly, we have problems. No one should ever expect to get through this world without adversity and each one is provided with a brain to apply, and not to think that we are in a Utopia where all our wants will be supplied on demand.
During 1957 and early 1958, most of the federal services located in my constituency
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy were moved elsewhere. This has brought great hardship upon a certain segment of the population and I would urge the departments concerned to co-operate in filling the gaps.
Most of camp Debert, including excellent air terminal facilities, have been vacated. This vacant camp area is well underlaid with miles of water mains and sewer mains, which could be utilized by other industry. There are also plenty of sources of water supply, railway siding facilities, air landing facilities, hangars and other buildings in the area. It is located very close to Truro on the main Canadian National Railways line, and I would urge this government to locate some type of crown corporation there or, if they have no intention of using this vacant area, to consider turning it over to other interests which might utilize it for industrial uses. I personally believe, and I suggest, that it should be turned over to the crown corporation of Nova Scotia known as Industrial Estates Limited, which is at this time doing such a wonderful job in promoting some industries in the province of Nova Scotia. The establishment of light industry not only in Debert but in other parts of the constituency would serve as well to absorb those displaced because of these changes and current slumps such as the depressed forest products industry.
There is another matter which requires immediate attention. The town of Windsor is located on the shores of the Avon river. At the present time part of this town is endangered by erosion. This river is subject to terrific tides and erosion has been taking place progressively in the town. Actually now the highest tides flow into some sections of the town. There are and there have been over the years some public works established on the river at that point. I suggest that they have made some contribution to the erosion here. I strongly urge that the government take some responsibility in providing some protection of this shore, otherwise, part of this town is going to suffer because it is impossible for the townspeople to assume the whole cost of such an undertaking.
Better transportation is one of the great needs of the maritimes. I am very proud that our local department of highways is making considerable improvements throughout the province of Nova Scotia. At the present time they are paying particular attention to the main highway linking Truro and Halifax. This highway is one of the most widely travelled in the province of Nova Scotia, and I would suggest that the whole highway will require the same treatment which sections of it are getting now. I would strongly urge that the provisions of the Trans-Canada Highway Act

Division
be extended to include this highway in order to help with the cost of construction of a highway which is so badly needed to handle the projected increase in the volume of traffic during the months and years to come.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to leave with you an observation. The sudden increase in the birth rate after the beginning of world war II has had a considerable impact upon our educational facilities. The burden of providing these facilities has fallen upon the present adult population. The impact of this terrific force will hit the labour force over the next few years. We, the present adult population, have moulded this force; they are our investment. Their opportunity is the greatest on this earth. I say, then, to the pressure groups of this country and the members of this house, let us not mislead them but rather let us encourage them to stand on their own feet. What these young people are inheriting was not built on dependence upon others but upon the initiative and courage of the individual. Training and leadership are essential so that our youth may face their careers with confidence. However, morale is not born of over dependence on others. I respectfully suggest, Mr. Speaker, that without morale no battle can be won.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the budget speech was delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), I have had the opportunity to meet many citizens from a few communities in the province of Quebec, and more particularly in my own riding. The majority of those people with whom I spoke were of Liberal allegiance, probably, because it is hardly possible by

now to find any supporters of the Conservative government. Indeed right thinking people in general are waking up from the great illusion that had been held out to them two years ago and they do not hesitate to express their dissatisfaction and disapproval of the Minister of Finance's budget.
There are ridings which, today, are happy not to have trusted the Conservative party. Those are the ridings where Liberal representatives were elected. It is true that we are not many, but we may boast to have freedom of speech, and sincerity of mind.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thanks to the Conservatives.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the Conservatives in the province of Quebec had the qualities I just quoted, they would not be afraid to say to the Canadian people, and more particularly the people in the province of Quebec, what they really think of the budget, as well as of the grants which have been doubled since the Conservative government is in power. I mean the grants to the provinces.
Some time ago an increase of $100 million was voted for the construction of highways in the province of Quebec. If Conservative members had been sincere, they would not have withdrawn behind the curtains but would have expressed their opinion here in this house. Their gesture was perhaps due to the attitude of the hon. member for Rober-val (Mr. Tremblay) who seems to have become the head of the Conservative members from the province of Quebec.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a matter I want to deal with more particularly on this occasion, namely the building of a bridge over the St. Lawrence at Three Rivers.
The idea is not new. A road crossing the river at that spot was already considered to be necessary in 1950 and there was some discussion whether a tunnel or a bridge would be preferable.
A few years later, in 1953, a group of sympathetic and able businessmen set up an organization with the aim of investigating the possibility of carrying out that project.
After a survey was made in Halifax, where a bridge had just been built crossing the river to the city of Dartmouth, it was revealed that an undertaking of that type in Three Rivers would be possible and would be self-liquidating.
A research fund of $30,000 was subscribed by the people concerned so that the project could be studied thoroughly.
The services of the consulting engineer for the Halifax bridge were retained, and Mr. P. L. Pratley, of Montreal, was instructed to make an extensive study of the project. In 66968-9-179
The Budget-Mr. Boulanger September 1954, he stated that the building of a bridge at Three Rivers was decidedly possible, that it would be self-liquidating and, furthermore, that there was great need of it.
The most elementary study of the immediate traffic and subsequent possibilities, he added, points to the urgent need of a better means of communication than ferryboats, not dependent upon weather conditions, seasons, winter ice, mechanical stallings and hazards of navigation.
After reading the Pratley report, the bridge committee felt reassured and hopeful. It decided to retain the services of a firm of consulting engineers from New York, Cover-dale and Colpitts, founded by a Canadian, Mr. W.H. Coverdale, to make a more elaborate study of the possibilities of the traffic anticipated.
That second report, published in November 1955, filled the bridge committee with optimism and enthusiasm.
The report stated that, during its first year of operation-it was believed then it would be in 1960-the traffic between the two shores would increase by 45 per cent; in the second year, by 10 per cent; and then, that it would continue to increase at an average rate of 5 per cent a year. At the toll rate established at the time of the investigation, they said, the bridge would be self-liquidating.
The cost of such a project had been estimated, at the time the plans were being prepared, at $12| million, which would have been financed through a 4J per cent interest loan, repayable in 13 or 14 years.
But at the time the first plans were accepted by the federal and provincial authorities, the seaway project necessitated a change in plans, which resulted in an increase of the estimates to $20 million, which would have then to be financed at a 6 and 6J per cent interest rate, in addition to higher cost of material, steel and labour.
Other studies were made on the self-paying possibilities of the project; it is still considered quite practicable. However, amortization would have to be on a period of 40 years, instead of 14, as was the case at the beginning.
Mr. Speaker, it has been established, beyond any doubt, by engineers and financiers, that the building of a bridge over the St. Lawrence at Three Rivers is a practicable and self-liquidating project in addition to being urgently required.
All the population of the Mauricie area and the eastern townships, all the manufacturers and farmers and everybody have been urging the construction of this bridge for many years.
2816	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Boulanger
I need hardly quote figures to prove this desire of almost half the population of the province of Quebec. The bridge would be located in the centre of the province and nobody, even those who would not benefit directly by it, would object to its construction since its cost would be financed not by taxes but by a private corporation.
In the course of certain debates of years past, here in this house and in political meetings, we have heard members who today are ministers make sensational statements in favour of the construction of that bridge.
The Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Balcer) himself, at the beginning of the 1953-54 session, made a speech from which I quote at page 65 of Hansard: Here is what the then member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) who today is the Solicitor General said:
At present, we are experiencing a lot of trouble with the ferry between Three Rivers and Ste. Angele. The system is so inadequate that one has to wait from three to four hours before being able to make the trip. And for this reason the national harbours board should improve the wharf at Three Rivers so that this city may become a modern port such as its geographical location would call for.
We have to face a large number of problems, but the number one problem undoubtedly is the joining of the north and south shores, by means of a bridge between Three Rivers and Ste. Angele in the county of Nicolet. This would help not only the city of Three Rivers, but all the cities in the district which are hampered by the lack of communications between the two shores. As a matter of fact, the whole central part of the province suffers from this state of affairs. It finds itself, because of that fact, in a state of economic inferiority.
And later he added:
That is why I ask the federal government to do its share, for it is a large-scale national undertaking.
The federal government collects a large proportion of the taxes. At the present time, it collects 77 per cent of the taxes so that there remains very little for the provinces and municipalities. The latter are in a precarious position, for real estate in the small towns cannot be taxed any more than it is now. Consequently cities and municipalities hesitate before embarking upon large-scale projects.
It was that same minister who, in a speech he made at the Ste. Cecile school in Three Rivers-that was of course, during the 1957 election campaign-made the following statement, as reported in Le Nouvelliste of Three Rivers on May 31, 1957. I quote:
The candidate added: "The matter of the bridge was raised during Mr. St. Laurent's visit. Mr. St. Laurent made the same reply as had been made


in 1908 by Mr. Laurier when the matter of building of a canal across the isthmus of Chignecto was being considered". According to Mr. Balcer, Mr. St. Laurent has only to utter the words "national necessity", and this means a first class burial for the bridge across the St. Lawrence.
Moreover, the federal government has insisted on two central spans for this bridge, which raises the cost by $7,000,000. Today, the promoters of the bridge have no way of raising this extra money. The federal government should pay the difference. At the same time, the people of all Canada will contribute to the St. Lawrence seaway, which will divert many ships from the port of Three Rivers. "The bridge will be a monument to the good sense of the people of Three Rivers", said Mr. Balcer. "No one should be allowed to play politics with such a matter".
True enough, Mr. Speaker, no one should play politics with this matter which is of interest to the people of between 15 and 20 constituencies, and it is time to prove it.
If the Solicitor General is true to his word, he will introduce a bill as soon as possible, thus giving effect to his high-sounding promises.
Think of the number of years the Solicitor General has been criticizing the Liberals, claiming they were opposed to the construction of this bridge.
Today, he is in a position of authority, in addition to having been pardoned for his disowning his leader at the 1956 convention.
Just what is it that is standing in the way of building the Three Rivers bridge?
Apparently, it is not Ottawa that is balking, because three federal cabinet ministers reportedly promised Ottawa's financial support to pay for the difference between the initial cost and the present cost, according to an item in Le Nouvelliste of March 4 last.
This report went on to say:
However, such promises are unofficial. It has been recognized that provincial government approval is an essential requirement. That, at least, was the main outcrop of the last general meeting of the chamber of commerce, held last week.
That organization thought it appropriate to pursue the matter by having the chairman of its bridge committee call on the premier of Quebec last February to sound him out. Mr. Duplessis expressed approval of the bridge in principle, but added that present economic conditions did not justify construction of the bridge at the present time.
The chamber of commerce and the people concerned do not agree with that view, however; they have expressed the opinion that it is never time to spend millions, but that faith in the future is often justification for bold undertakings.
The studies and surveys made by the people concerned show that there is still an obstacle which stands in the way of the building of the Three Rivers bridge and only the premier of the province of Quebec can overcome it by

a simple approval, which would be of no serious consequence, and by guaranteeing the first year's operational deficit, as was done in the case of the Halifax bridge. It is the responsibility of federal and provincial members to act jointly and to put pressure on the provincial authorities so that they give their approval. A suggestion was made in the Three Rivers chamber of commerce to the effect that provincial members of the legislative assembly from the 15 counties in the central area of Quebec would be asked to stake their seat on the proposed bridge that would span the river at Three Rivers.
This shows the determination of the promoters, of the chamber of commerce, of the Three Rivers city council and of the citizens who subscribed $30,000 for the use of the research committee.
When workers are desperately looking for jobs, this undertaking could not be more timely.
Unlike the premier of the province of Quebec, we submit the implementation of such a project I just told you about will improve the economic situation.
