subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before tackling my main theme, 1 would like to tell of the impression I have of this house after listening for a whole year to hon. members of the loyal opposition.
To my mind, the reason for which the people of Canada got rid of the Liberals, was that it realized, after several years, that it was made up only of practical jokers. We may wonder, Mr. Speaker, who is the greater clown, the hon. member for Bonavista-66968-9-179J
The Budget-Mr. Parizeau Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) or the latest arrival in this house, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis).
This reminds me somewhat of some happenings during the last world war. You will surely recall them, Mr. Speaker. When there was intensive training in England, the famous Lord Haw! Haw! used to say: "The Mac-Naughton circus is on the run again". Well.. I am saying: "The Pearson circus in on the run again. Yes, the Pearson circus is on the run again and it will be on the run for quite a while."
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the government through the distinguished Minister of Finance, for well-balanced budget he has just presented to the Canadian people. In times as difficult and complicated as these, legislation brought in by our government will help reduce unemployment and check inflation.
The people of Lake St. John asked me to thank the government for everything that has been done since it took over in this country, and more particularly for all that has been done in the building field. As a matter of fact, the sound action taken under the National Housing Act has helped a great number of workers in my riding, as anywhere else in Canada, to become homeowners.
I am speaking in full knowledge of the case because in 1956, only about 60 homes had been built at Alma, our county town, whereas that figure has gone up to 85 in 1957 and to a record high of 126 last year. The people of Lake St. John owe those magnificent results to the government, Mr. Speaker, as the necessary legislation was passed to facilitate loans to help our workers.
However, Mr. Speaker, economists and experts agree that while there has been considerable improvement in the National Housing Act, following legislation introduced by this government, more should be done radically to solve the housing crisis which, it must be said, is still critical throughout the country, but to a varying degree.
The problem of home ownership, is, as we have all learned, the crux of the social problem, as it constitutes the basis of this nation's prosperity. For the last few years, we have to face all sorts of concepts and theories, aimed at destroying and sapping the principles we have been taught. Those nefarious ideas have greater impact on people who are not attached by owners' rights, and that is why we must tackle the problem boldly and find adequate solutions. Among those which we feel are the most practicable and possible, there is one which should

The Budget-Mr. Parizeau particularly draw the attention of our government, and that is that each citizen should be provided with a house of his own.
If we take a look at history, Mr. Speaker, we realize at once that revolutions in the old countries were organized and directed by people who did not enjoy the benefits of property rights. It was then a struggle between tenants or slaves against owners or lords. We have not yet reached that point, and I am far from believing that we could ever reach it. However, it is on account of a lack of foresight on the part of government leaders that peoples could rise and follow the lead of revolutionaries.
Mr. Speaker, our government has already shown great vision in adopting adequate social measures to stem the wave of unemployment which was spreading all over the country. Its housing policy has been of great help to our people, thus checking unemployment, but especially in the fight against subversive ideas, by providing easy means of obtaining money to those who wanted to become owners.
Property is the basic element in the development of the individual; it is basic to the existence and welfare of the family, and contributes to social peace. There will not be better defenders of our country than our own people, once they are owners. Our country should be a land of predilection, where the old saying would be truer than anywhere else: "To each his home, to each his little tract of land, and the country will be safe."
Those who thrive on overtly spreading liberal or socialist doctrines seek above all to attack private property. It is up to us therefore to defend it, if we want our ideas and principles to be listened to and followed by the people.
I am sure that we will succeed, if we keep on helping construction by voting still larger sums of money for house building in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind you of an idea I put forward last year at the time of the debate on the speech from the throne, for the further improvement of that housing loan act. In fact, as recorded on page 649 of Hansard of May 29, 1958, I said that the interest rates should be lowered, in order to help Canadian workers, since they are unable to pay $75 or $80 a month for capital and interest charges.
I repeat the same suggestion this year, Mr. Speaker, asking again a lowering of the in-


terest rates in favour of the borrower who is building a house through the C.M.H.C. The 6 per cent interest now being paid by the borrower is much too high, because its cost, over a period of 25 years, almost doubles the initial amount of the loan, which is hardly the purpose of the act.
Allow me to digress briefly at this point to say that the citizens of the Saguenay-Lake St. Jean area are seriously affected by the lay-off of employees of the Aluminum Company of Canada, a lay-off which has been brought on by the lack of markets and the cut-throat competition of iron curtain countries. The company intends to rehire these people as soon as possible. Meanwhile, however, they are unable to meet their obligations. I therefore urge the government to take whatever steps are needed to enable these people to renew their contract with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and to have the privilege of paying an extra $5 or $10 when they resume their work, instead of having to catch up on their rent payments in a single shot. I was therefore saying that a means must be found to reduce the interest rate, and this without altering the national budget, so as to enable more people with low incomes to become home owners, a privilege to which they are entitled just as anyone else.
If you look at the statistics, you will find that 163,000 houses were built in Canada last year. Had the interest rate been 3 per cent, for instance, rather than 6 per cent, it would have meant a saving of close to $5 million for the taxpayers who became property owners in the last year. At that rate, it adds up to the fabulous figure of $125 million over a period of 25 years, a saving that would enable many Canadians to become home owners.
I have no thought of dictating to the government, but as a suggestion, may I be allowed to outline a plan that might result in considerable improvement of the construction situation? I would suggest, as I indicated last year, reducing the interest rate by 3 per cent, and this without interfering with the national budget.
To this end, I would first suggest amending the Criminal Code to allow for setting up a national lottery such as exists in other countries. However, the entire proceeds from this national lottery, under government control, would be made available to the Central

Housing and Mortgage Corporation Fund as a means of reducing the interest rate. Such a measure would be of considerable benefit, because the government would have no outlay to face as a means of reducing the interest rate. It would only have to keep making regular annual payments as a help to construction.
It would be an innovation, Mr. Speaker, and may be a revolution in our way of life, but we must follow the march of progress. According to surveys made by responsible agencies, 95 per cent of the population would be in favour of a national lottery and those who would oppose all games of chance would only mildly object.
Should we not keep in Canada the millions of dollars that are going out of the country each year on lotteries? Mr. Speaker, I would be interested to know how many hon. members have, at times, bought a lottery ticket; it was the simple psychological effect of the man who takes a chance, without any ulterior motive. But is not life itself a continuous game of chance, Mr. Speaker? The insurance we buy on our life, on the life of our family, on our house, our car, are all chances that we take, are they not? We take chances every day and I do say that there are many people here who take chances with much more consequences than if they would buy a simple lottery ticket.
I would like to go into more details about the effects of a national lottery as an aid to housing. Considering that we could build as many as 400,000 houses a year to meet the immediate needs of the population, this could mean about $120 million in interest, a sum that we could return to the new owners with a reduction of 3 per cent in the rate of interest on average loans of $10,000.
That return of interest of $120 million would be entirely covered, I am sure, by the revenues of a national lottery which, I believe, for the sake of argument, could easily reach $150 million. Thus, the national budget would not be affected by this reduction of interest and it would be of considerable help to the new owners.
Mr. Speaker, it would be the best way to resist these subversive movements which try to infiltrate our country. It is proclaimed everywhere that that property thrives on exaggeration, that it must be overthrown and destroyed. Pope Leo XIII gave us the answer
The Budget-Mr. Parizeau to these ideas in his encyclical letter Rerum Novarum, when he said:
Socialists condemn the poor to jealous hatred of those who possess; they claim that all ownership must be abolished, that each man's possessions should be common property and that their administration must be vested in the municipality or the state.
So, that is what we have to fight, Mr. Speaker, by all possible means, even by a national lottery, if necessary. This reminds me of the story of the good communist who, trying to explain the communist doctrine to one of his friends, told him: "It is simple; I am going to explain it to you. Suppose that you have ten cows, you give me five; that is the communist doctrine. Suppose that you have twenty sheep, you give me ten; that is the communist doctrine. Suppose that you have fifty chickens, and you give me twenty-five." "Oh! No", replies the friend. "I have no cows nor sheep, but I have chickens, so I'm going to keep them."
This is the answer we are looking for, Mr. Speaker. The man who owns something has no intention of sharing; he is master in his home, he is conscious of his strength and proud to be a good citizen, a true Canadian.
In closing my remarks and as an example, I am pleased to mention my own city of Alma, in my constituency of Lake St. John, where the number of home owners increased from 35 per cent in 1953 to 51 per cent in 1958. Here is a city that benefited of the advantages offered by the government in the field of home building, but it is also a city where every citizen has the ambition to own his home in order to be a better Canadian. People of that kind, we would need hundreds of thousands more of them every year, and it is the duty of the government to take necessary action in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, we belong to a party that is still young but has noble and high ambitions. We all want to make Canada a prosperous country. Home building is a way to bring about this result, while reducing employment at the same time.
I am sincere, Mr. Speaker, when I state that we must do even more in order that everyone may own his property, that everyone may be proud to own a small part of our country. I ask therefore that the government take note of my suggestion and consider it on its merits, because it represents the thought of thousands and thousands of Canadians.

The Budget-Mr. Brassard

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my friend the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Parizeau) has put forward at least one idea I can support, with respect to national lotteries. I fail to see why there is so much hypocrisy on this matter. Many people who are anxious to take on a holier-than-thou attitude object to the idea of a national lottery in this country, but how many, on the other hand, at home or between the four walls of an office, make no bones about buying lottery tickets, thus helping to send overseas millions of dollars from which hospitals and educational institutions of other countries derive a great benefit. I submit a national lottery could help the housing industry, as was said by my friend the hon. member for Lake St. John, and could also have a beneficial effect in the field of education in the province of Quebec.
I have listened to a good number of Conservative members who took part in the budget debate and all of them of course congratulated the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for introducing a courageous budget on April 9 last.
Not so long ago a Conservative member said in this house that the Canadian people had welcomed the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance. Such a statement sounds queer when you take cognizance of the recent newspaper reports on this matter. For instance the Ottawa Citizen on April 16, 1959, carried a story entitled:
(Text):
Survey of the Press Shows Budget Critically Received
The Toronto Star, of course, was critical. (Translation):
I would just like to refer to two or three comments made by newspapers in order to prove perhaps our colleagues have no monopoly on truth.
For instance in the Toronto Star, we can read the following:
(Text):
It said that one thing was sure about the budget, namely, "it has dissolved the last vestige of the financial mythology created by Mr. Diefenbaker before the 1957 election. He promised to raise welfare payments, cut taxes and balance the budget. The payments were raised, taxes cut. and the result of these things plus the recession was the biggest deficit in our peacetime history. Now Mr. Fleming finds it necessary to raise taxes by an amount which exceeds his previous tax relief by nearly $150 million a year. So much for financial magic."
In neighbouring Hamilton, the Spectator said that "although Mr. Fleming told the commons
(Mr. Parizeau.]
that his budget was designed 'to foster and promote recovery,' its fiscal details suggest no such positive purpose."
And along in Windsor, the Star took a roundhouse swing in Mr. Fleming's direction. "The blunt fact", said the Star, "is that the Conservative government has been spending far in excess of any Canadian government, even in wartime, and much further in excess of its revenues than any government in peacetime. Where does it think such a policy will lead? If a private individual were to follow the same practice he would be headed for speedy bankruptcy."
Out on Canada's west coast the Vancouver Sun was outspokenly critical. "Canadians now know what value to put on a Tory election promise. They were promised lower taxes and they have got higher taxes... when a patient is recovering the wise physician coddles the body. Mr. Fleming compels his patient, the Canadian economy, to don a hair shirt."
The Victoria Times had this ironic comment: "It is a courageous budget, since it admits that the government completely miscalculated the nation's finances and misled the public with impossible promises in two elections... The government is showing a new sense of responsibility. It is late but welcome."
Like the Star-Phoenix's line that the "Diefenbaker vision must be taking on the dimensions of a nightmare," the Winnipeg Free Press trumpeted, not surprisingly in an editorial called "Cost Of The Vision," that the Canadian people had been handed "the second instalment of the bill for the vision. And a shocker it was."
(Translation):
Among the Conservative members who took part in the debate and praised the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance, I want to refer particularly to the Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) who made a brilliant speech.
I was a bit surprised when I heard him commend the government the way he did, and I wondered if he had not already spoken in this house about the problems that confront us to-day. Therefore, I leafed through Hansard from the previous years and I found out that on March 6, 1950, as we can see on page 520, the Secretary of State who was then sitting in the opposition had risen about the question of unemployment; however in 1950, unemployment was far, very far from reaching its present day proportions and still here are the words, quite-I shall not say courageous-but critical, he used concerning the administration then in power. Thus, I quote from Hansard of March 6, 1950, on page 520. These are the words of the present Secretary of State:
Mr. Chairman, let us not forget that unemployment is the breeding ground of disorder, poverty, unrest and communism. Unemployment leads to communism. It must therefore be averted. We have tried to fight it with words but that was a wasted, futile, useless effort. People do not yet understand why there was so much employment and money in wartime and why there is so little now, in peacetime. If money is found for destructive ends, it should also be available for constructive purposes. Should the fact that consumers are too few in number justify starvation in the homes of the jobless?

And a little further on, the hon. member said:
I therefore ask the government to attend to these alarming wounds, to heal them. That is within its powers as well as within its duties. There is no reason why any one of our citizens should not be able to live in a country 3,700,000 square miles in area.
In my own name, in that of my constituency, of my province-
The hon. member used high-sounding words at the time.
- (in the name) of my own race, in the name of the whole country which is threatened with the same crisis, the same miseries, I beseech those in power to put an end to this sad state of affairs.
Let us find jobs for our people. That is the only way to earn a salary. Whatever work is found, let it be, not just any work, but useful work, constructive work which will benefit our country. Let us not fight communism with words, but with action, honestly, by ensuring to the people what is rightfully theirs-order, justice, prosperity and national security in this fine, powerful and great country of ours.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-5, to amend the Small Loans Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we all seem to be good-natured this afternoon and there seems to be an unusual amount of co-operation on procedural matters which I think is all to the good. However, when the division bells ring that co-operation ceases to exist.
I have moved second reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker, because I feel that the interest rates now being charged by small loans companies in this country are unnecessarily high. The small loans business is very extensive.

Small Loans Act
Hundreds of thousands of Canadians avail themselves of such loans, and I submit to the house that a maximum rate of interest of 1 per cent per month should be ample at the present time. Following the amendments adopted in 1956 the maximum rate for loans up to $300 has been 2 per cent per month. The amendment provided by this bill would place a ceiling of 1 per cent per month on all interest rates charged by small loans companies.
I have had similar bills on the order paper every year since 1955, and although experience under this new administration would seem to suggest that private members' bills and resolutions are becoming of less and less value, nevertheless the experience I have had with regard to this particular bill has indicated to me that it has been very worth while and that parliament has listened. In 1956 the government acted. I did not think the legislation at that time went nearly far enough. The original proposal I made prior to action being taken by the government in 1956 was along these same lines. Before 1956 the rates on loans up to $500 were controlled by the Small Loans Act by providing a maximum ceiling of 2 per cent month.
This particular measure has never received, either by way of vote or speech, strong support from any member of either the Liberal or Conservative parties, but in 1956, because public opinion demanded that action be taken and because the minister of finance at that time, the Hon. Walter Harris, was in this instance paying some attention to public opinion, action was taken. As a result of that action many millions of dollars have been saved the consumers of this country.
When the government's bill, going part way along the road I had suggested, was before the banking and commerce committee in 1956 numerous representatives attended from the small loans companies. There were spokesmen for the small loans companies association and spokesmen for individual companies. Crocodile tears were shed by members of the Conservative and Liberal parties and initially not all members of the Liberal party were in favour of the government's legislation. They were worrying about the widows and poor people who would have to have loans but would no longer be able to get them because conditions were going to be so difficult for this gang of loan sharks incorporated with the blessing of the government.
What has the result been? They have not suffered. They have prospered and grown.
tMr. Argue.]
They have extended their business. They have made an increasing amount of profit. They have done very well. Perhaps this was the kind of legislation which was necessary to suggest to them that they should increase their volume of business. By increasing their volume of business at somewhat lower rates of interest they have been able to effect an even higher net profit than theretofore. I know that if this bill were placed before the banking and commerce committee at this time the small loans companies would come before the committee once again in droves and would plead that they would be crippled if this legislation were passed. But I suggest that if it is passed, as it should be, those companies would prosper under what I consider to be a very ample rate, yes, a very high rate, of 1 per cent per month.
We had the men in the grey flannel suits before the committee; I think 50 of them came in 1956. There was a tremendous lobby and not without some effect, because it took the greatest possible amount of persuasion by the minister of finance. I think the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson) will remember the occasion very well. The minister of finance was determined, and finally some of the members of the Liberal party who were reluctant to go along with the minister voted the right way and the Conservatives took to their heels and quit the opposition which they had initially started in that committee.
With the government we now have, I see no indication that there is so much as a single member on the government side of the house who is prepared to stand up and say that he supports action by the government to lower the interest rates on small loans companies.

The purpose of this legislation is to provide that interest or the cost of a loan allowable under the Small Loans Act shall not exceed the aggregate of 1 per cent per month on any part of the unpaid principal balance not exceeding $1,000 and one-half of one per cent per month on any remainder of the unpaid principal balance exceeding $1,000.
I should like briefly to discuss the history of small loans companies in this country. In the early stages of the development of Canada each family was a largely independent unit and produced its own needs. Family units were relatively independent of outside

Small Loans Act
sources. However, there was a gradual change from a crop economy to a cash economy. This was prompted by the movement of citizens from the farms to the cities and towns. Families became dependent upon a cash income and any interruption or emergency that reduced the family budget caused a serious crisis and hence a need arose for sources of small sum credit. The existing laws at that time were ineffective to deal with moneylenders because the legislation did not take into consideration the changed conditions and did not protect the public from unscrupulous lenders. Consequently rates of 400 and 500 per cent were quite common. People could not repay these short term loans-weekly or monthly loans -and in the final analysis paid many times the amount of the loan in interest over a period of a year or more and still had the principal amount to repay.
The legislation concerning interest was ineffective at that time for two reasons. First, the borrower was in a poor bargaining position and second, as I have mentioned, certain charges for such things as investigations or the preparation of documents were permitted legally because only the interest rate was controlled.
This was the situation that obtained during the mid-thirties. The Moneylenders Act which was in force at that time restricted the rate of interest on loans up to $500 to 12 per cent per annum but no restriction was placed on various other charges that could be made. In 1938 the House of Commons committee on banking and commerce made a report which formed the basis of the Small Loans Act. This plugged the gap and provided a rate to include all charges, including interest. The rate established was 2 per cent per month on loans up to $500. The rate applied each month after the monthly payments of principal and interest had been made.
In 1956 the act was again amended because most operators were now making loans up to $1,500 in value and so the present rates were established at that time. The rates that are in effect today are 2 per cent per month on that part of the unpaid principal balance up to $300, 1 per cent over $300 to $1,000, and one-half of one per cent over $1,000 up to $1,500. It is possible that at this time we should have another look at this legislation. Perhaps in this day and age these rates are somewhat high. However, I am not prepared to accept the words or opinions of the hon. member for Assiniboia because I do not feel that he has done the research into this matter that he might have done.

What he has given us this afternoon are opinions and not facts. I should like to point out to the house that another bill placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Assiniboia would provide that interest rates under the Interest Act could not exceed 12 per cent. I merely point out that the two bills conflict with one another. The combined effect is that the licensed lenders under the Small Loans Act would be allowed a lower rate of interest than the unlicensed lenders. The unlicensed lenders could charge a rate of 1 per cent per month while the licensed lenders would only be able to charge a combination of 1 per cent and one-half of one per cent per month. This would be a reversal of the principle that the smaller the loan the higher the rate needs to be. Here I should like to quote from the report of the committee on banking and commerce which was presented to the House of Commons in 1938:
Quite obviously the purchase of a block of 12-year Canadian government bonds requires little expenditure for investigation and none for supervision: investments in 50 farm mortgages for varied periods entail considerable cost both for investigation and supervision; while the investigation of 1,000 applications to effect loans to 500 people for a few months with meticulous supervision becomes expensive business when expressed as a percentage rate of $100 on a monthly basis.
I submit that the hon. member for Assiniboia, by presenting these two bills which conflict with one another, is not quite sure in his own mind as to just what the problem is, let alone what the remedy should be.
I should also like to point out to the hon. member that a great many of the people who do business with small loans companies seem to be quite satisfied with their dealings. I am informed by the president of one of the large finance companies that in 1957 the figures for his company show that over 90 per cent of the loans made were to people who had dealt with them before or who had been referred by others who had dealt with them.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Smith), I am in general agreement with the tenor of the bill and agree that certainly interest rates charged by small loans companies, as by other concerns, should be no higher than necessary. I support this bill to the extent that certainly an inquiry should be made, and that the interest chargeable by small loans companies should be limited to the extent necessary to provide funds for the availability of people who cannot borrow from other loan sources. However, it is a matter which should be examined very carefully because, as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has neglected to consider, there is a very good possibility that by limiting the interest on loans by small companies, as he suggests, it would deprive the wage earner and the man who is unable to borrow at banks or from other institutions, of funds that he needs and requires in his daily routine.
I think that one of the most important aspects of the whole problem of consumer financing and the business done by finance companies has been neglected by this bill. Certainly, it has always been an accepted principle that the interest rate charged should be in relation to the risk of the loan. And that has been the argument the finance companies have used to justify interest rates which are much higher than would be charged by banks or other institutions. But it seems to me, that at least in one instance in the consumer finance field this argument has no jurisdiction whatever. I refer to the large amount of consumer financing that is dene through acceptance corporations; that is to say, the very large finance corporations which do not make loans directly to the purchaser, but which lend him the money through the dealer or the retailer from whom he purchases an automobile, appliance or other goods.
We have been striving in this nation, as other free nations, for stability in the money that is available in the country; to try to control booms and prevent busts. We do that through the Bank of Canada which was established by the Bennett government in 1934. It has been done by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in the budget which he introduced last week. The amount of money available in the nation at any given time will affect the expansion and the amount of production in the nation.
It seems to me that consumer finance companies in some cases make available an unhealthy type of credit in the nation, a

Small Loans Act
credit that oftentimes in periods of inflation is greatly expanded when it should not be. Many consumers are thereby invited to purchase goods and through advertising programs are encouraged to seek loans which they cannot afford. In the case of an automobile dealer who recommends a finance company to his customer, the acceptance corporation or the finance company may charge interest rates considerably higher than those that would be charged by a bank. At the same time the finance company may take much less risk than the bank takes.
The acceptance corporation has not only the security of the article which has been sold, the car, television set or any other type of appliance, but also has the security of the endorsement of the consumer and the endorsement of the retailer. These companies take little risk, yet they charge high risk interest rates. Since they assume small risk they are ready to make money available at any time, often at times when the nation cannot absorb it, and some people are encouraged to buy goods which they cannot afford. It seems to me that these acceptance corporations should be required to assume the risk themselves on the money they lend. They should be precluded from requiring the endorsement of the retailer or the dealer. If they are going to charge these interest rates, at least let them accept the risk on the loan.

Question
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Were instructions issued some time in March, 1958, by the legal branch of the Montreal regional office of the Unemployment Insurance Commission for an investigation to be carried out in Sherbrooke regarding the payment to certain textile workers of unemployment insurance benefits to which they were not entitled?
2.	Did any employees receive overpayments?
3.	If so, what was the amount overpaid in each case?
4.	Was the investigation stopped?
5.	How was the matter settled by the commission?
6.	Were these employees compelled to refund such overpayments?
Answer by: Hon. Michael Siarr (Minister of
Labour):
1.	Yes, when it was reported to the Montreal regional office that several claimants had omitted to disclose as earnings the amounts of production bonuses received from their former employer.
2.	Yes; overpayments were established in 442 cases.
3.	Full information is not available but the amounts ranged from $1.00 to $168.00 with the bulk under $50 each.
4.	No, the investigation was carried to conclusion.
5.	Claimants who were overpaid were required to make restitution. In a few cases other infractions were discovered as a result of the investigation and punitive action was taken with regard to them.
6.	See answer to No. 5.

Monday, April 20, 1959
